World.title: 450K borrowers say they were ripped off. Their student loans are being erased
World.content:
450K borrowers say they were ripped off. Their student loans are being erased

toggle caption Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

The long legal battle to erase the debts of nearly half a million federal student loan borrowers who say they were defrauded by their colleges is finally coming to an end, after a recent court ruling in a lawsuit that has spanned three presidential administrations.

The class-action suit, originally filed against the first Trump administration seven years ago, centered on a federal rule known as borrower defense. The rule is supposed to allow borrowers to petition the U.S. Education Department to erase their debts if a school has lied to them — about things like their job prospects, their credits' transferability or their likely salary after graduation.

Sponsor Message

During Trump's first term, thousands of borrowers who claimed they had been ripped off by predatory schools waited years to have their borrower defense claims reviewed. Finally, advocates sued, arguing that, under then-Education Secretary Betsy DeVos, the department had deliberately and illegally stopped processing claims and wrongfully denied others without considering the merits of their cases.

The suit has endured long enough to bear the names of three different education secretaries: from Sweet v. DeVos in 2019 to Sweet v. Cardona during the Biden administration, and now Sweet v. McMahon for Trump's second term.

"At the end of the day, this settlement has impacted over 450,000 people, and it's improved their personal balance sheets by over $23 billion," said Eileen Connor, executive director of the Project on Predatory Student Lending (PPSL), the advocacy group that filed the suit against the department in 2019.

Once all of the required loan discharges and refunds are completed, Connor says the Sweet settlement will be the largest ever against the U.S. government.

Why it has taken so long

In 2022, the Biden administration agreed to a landmark settlement in the class-action suit, pledging that borrowers who had attended a predetermined list of more than 150 mostly for-profit colleges would receive full and automatic relief from their loans.

Sponsor Message

Not only that, but the settlement also allowed more than 250,000 additional borrowers to apply for relief during a brief, post-settlement period in 2022. It required the department to review those new claims within a set period of time or the loans in question would have to be discharged.

The second Trump administration revealed in court documents that it had processed only 60,000 of those post-class applications by the court-appointed deadline.

The current Education Department has argued in court that it needs more time — 18 months — to properly review so many applications, "ensuring that taxpayer funds are only disbursed to those borrowers who are entitled to relief on the merits."

But, in a July 17 ruling that likely means the end of this legal fight, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit told the department that the obligations of the settlement were clear early on — and yet the department waited three years to raise an objection.

Ellen Keast, an Education Department spokesperson, told NPR in a statement that the Sweet settlement "imposed an unrealistic deadline."

She said, "The Department has complied in good faith with court orders, and we believe the court erred in not granting our reasonable request."

"I'm really angry about all the years that my family suffered under these loans"

Jessica Feindt is one of the post-class borrowers who's been waiting years for relief. She lives near Flint, Mich., and was one of the first in her family to go to college. She enrolled at University of Phoenix, hoping to earn an undergraduate degree in psychology.

"They really marketed heavily in the area. It was on every radio station, every newspaper. It was everywhere," Feindt says.

Feindt did earn her degree — and in less than four years. But she took out a lot of debt to do so. "I paid a lot out of pocket. I paid through student loans. I had all federal loans because poor people cannot get [private] loans."

But, she says, she realized later that the school's recruitment counselor had repeatedly misled her, including telling her that her degree would be accepted by the Michigan graduate programs she was interested in applying to next. It wasn't. In 2022, she filed a borrower defense claim, joining that post-settlement group.

Sponsor Message

In court documents filed in April as part of its appeal, the Education Department revealed that, after the Sweet settlement of 2022, it had provided some $12 billion in loan discharges and/or refunds to nearly 300,000 federal student loan borrowers who claimed to have been defrauded. After the July ruling, that dollar amount will continue to grow considerably.

Connor likens this case, about schools defrauding borrowers, to the historic settlement against Big Tobacco. Like cigarettes, she says, these student loans to predatory schools are "toxic products."

Less than a week ago, Feindt logged in to her federal student loan account, and her college debts were gone — erased soon after the latest developments in the Sweet case.

"I feel like I should be happy," Feindt says, "but I'm really angry about all the years that my family suffered under these loans."

Edited by: Nicole Cohen

Research by: Will Chase

World.title: WestJet to begin parking planes ahead of possible strike
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WestJet is beginning to park its 737 aircraft across its network as the clock ticks closer to a possible strike by the airline's flight attendants.

The airline says this measure will help prevent travellers and planes from being stranded abroad.

"This necessary step allows the airline to maintain operational control and protect the integrity of the broader network," WestJet said in an update on its website.

The airline says passengers should check the status of their flight before leaving for the airport.

Despite the wind down, the company said it was still bargaining with flight attendants in order to try and reach a negotiated deal.

WestJet's flight attendants issued a 72-hour strike notice Thursday, which the airline responded to with a 72-hour lockout notice of their own. That means some 4,287 flight attendants could be off the job as soon as Sunday at 12:01 a.m. MT — over the August long weekend, a busy time for domestic travel.

That strike notice doesn't commit flight attendants to taking job action, but has proved worrisome for passengers who are left in limbo, unsure whether or not their flights will take off this weekend.

The airline says WestJet Encore flights and codeshare flights operated by airline partners remain unaffected.

WATCH | WestJet strike could cost this traveller up to $20K: WestJet strike could cost this traveller up to $20K | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 10:39 WestJet flight attendants have issued a 72-hour strike notice, raising the possibility of a walkout during the busy summer travel season. Bonnie Thompson says a cancelled trip could leave her out as much as $20,000 in prepaid expenses.

In two emails obtained by CBC News, WestJet said it had put forward what it believes is the best agreement it could responsibly offer.

That includes an agreement to the union's request for compensation before and after flights through "duty premium payments," a cumulative wage increase of about 36 per cent over four years, scheduling improvements and better provisions for things like travel and hotels while flight attendants are away from home, according to a WestJet email.

"The offer would have represented a significant step forward not only for WestJet Cabin Crew, but for the Canadian airline industry as a whole," one of the emails reads in part.

CBC News reached out to the union, known as the CUPE WestJet Component, for comment.

Union hopeful strike can be avoided

In response to the emails, CUPE WestJet Component President Alia Hussain said what WestJet has shared is a "small part of a very large contract."

"We aren’t just bargaining a few things, we are seeking a comprehensive contract that reflects the priorities of our members," Hussain said in an email.

Hussain added that while some progress has been made toward reaching a deal, there are issues remaining that "need to be resolved at the table."

"We are hopeful that we can still avoid a strike and remain committed to resolving this there."

WestJet declined an interview with CBC News, saying its leaders are focused on the negotiations.

A key issue at the heart of negotiations has been ground pay.

Flight attendants say an average of 35 hours per month go unpaid under WestJet's current "credit hour" system. That pay structure compensates flight attendants for ground duties, delays and other required work by paying them a set amount of credit hours per flight, which can change depending on the trip.

WestJet says the credit system is standard in the industry, and it argues flight attendants are paid at a higher rate under this pay structure in order to compensate for additional duties during what flight attendants consider unpaid time.

WATCH | WestJet passengers scramble after flight attendants give strike notice: WestJet passengers scramble after flight attendants give strike notice | Duration 2:51 WestJet passengers are scrambling to make new arrangements after thousands of flight attendants issued a 72-hour strike notice, to which the airline responded with a lockout notice. Flight attendants could be off the job by Sunday if no new deal is reached.

Still, the company's CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech has said WestJet is aware that many employees are unhappy with the current pay system, and says they are willing to make changes as long as they are financially feasible for the company.

WestJet has said that passengers who booked directly with the airline will be notified of any changes, and those who booked through a third party like a travel agent should make changes through that agency directly.

Passengers with flights booked between now and Aug. 4 are still able to cancel or change their flights, though doing so might only net them a travel credit rather than their money back directly.

World.title: Health Canada drops final barriers to sperm donation by gay and bisexual men
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Aziz M. says becoming a sperm donor is the best decision he ever made — and he hopes other gay and bisexual men will now have the opportunity to do the same.

The Toronto man, whose full name is protected by a publication man, was the plaintiff in a three-year legal battle with Health Canada over what he believes were discriminatory criteria for sperm donation.

But on Thursday, the agency said it will drop questions about sexual behaviour from its screening process, eliminating a barrier that precluded many gay and bisexual men from donating.

"I'm very happy," Aziz told As It Happens guest host Loren McInnis. "I'm hoping a lot more queer men would go and donate."

Starting this fall, Health Canada says it will no longer ask potential sperm donors whether they have recently had anal sex with a new partner or one of multiple partners.

LISTEN | Interview with Aziz M. about new sperm donation rules: As It Happens 6:36 Health Canada drops barriers to sperm donation by gay and bisexual men 3 years into legal challenge Aziz M. was the plaintiff at the heart of a three-year legal battle with Health Canada over what he believes were discriminatory criteria for sperm donation. Now, that battle is over, and Aziz is celebrating. He spoke to As It Happens guest host Loren McInnis.

All donors, the department says, will still be rigorously screened for infectious diseases, such as HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C.

Health Canada says it made the changes after consulting with stakeholders in the field of assisted reproduction.

"The Government of Canada is committed to making sure that sperm and ova donation policies are safe, non-discriminatory and based on scientific evidence," the agency said in an emailed statement.

Policy based on stereotypes, advocates say

Egale Canada, a 2SLGBTQ+ charity that was going to act as an intervener in the case, welcomed the news.

"This case presented an important opportunity to examine long-standing assumptions about sexual orientation in relation to HIV, and how these policies must be grounded and assessed through the lens of Charter rights," Bennett Jensen, Egale's legal director, said in an emailed statement.

Bennett Jensen, director of legal for Egale Canada, welcomes Health Canada's policy change. (Submitted by Egale Canada)

When Aziz started donating sperm in 2014, he wasn't yet out and sexually active as a gay man.

About 10 years ago, a family used his donated sperm to conceive a child. That child, he says, has been a part of his life ever since.

"I had a wonderful experience ... and it has enriched my life immensely," he said. "I then told other people, especially queer friends, about this experience and encouraged them, you know, to give it a shot."

But it turns out that many of them couldn't.

Before 2024, Health Canada explicitly banned sperm donations by men who have had sex with men within the three months prior to donation, citing an increased risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.

"It kind of reminded me of all the prejudice that we gay and bisexual men get in life and all the negative opinions that society often holds against us," Aziz said.

"It felt like it was a group judgment. Like, anybody from that group is having, you know, risky sexual behaviour and they're diseased."

In 2023, he launched a constitutional challenge against the policy. In response, Health Canada ended its blanket ban on donations from men who have sex with men in 2024 , then tweaked its screening language to make questions about anal sex gender neutral.

Aziz and his lawyers welcomed the move but decided to forge ahead with their case anyway.

"It actually switched an explicit discrimination to an implicit one," Aziz said. "The same group of people are more likely to be disqualified."

Experts say testing and quarantine are enough

Receptive anal intercourse has been identified as a risk factor for many sexually transmitted infections. But three medical experts who submitted affidavits in the case say Health Canada's physical screening process is thorough enough to weed out any dangers.

Every sperm donation is tested for infectious disease when first collected, quarantined for a minimum of 180 days and then tested again before release.

"Current HIV testing methods are highly sensitive and accurate, such that there is effectively no residual risk associated with current testing methods," Dr. Mona Loutfy, a Toronto-based infectious disease physician, wrote in an affidavit for the case.

Dr. Mona Loutfy, an infectious disease specialist with expertise in HIV and reproductive medicine, filed an affidavit in support of removing the barriers to donation faced by men who have sex with men. (CBC)

Emily McIntosh, executive director of the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society, agrees. Her organization, which represents scientists and health-care workers in the field of assisted reproduction, was also scheduled to be an intervener in the case.

"This is quite rigorous, and asking somebody about their behaviour is in fact moot," she said. "Not to mention the fact that that's assuming everybody is answering all questions fully truthfully or to the best of their knowledge."

Research published last year in the journal Transfusion found questionnaires are an ineffective way to screen blood donors, as participants often choose not to disclose key information.

More sperm donors needed

McIntosh says the new rules are good news for people trying to start families through assisted reproduction. Because it's illegal in Canada to pay for donated sperm and ova, she says there aren't enough sperm donors to meet the need.

Aziz says he hopes the new rules will encourage more gay and bisexual men to donate.

"For a lot of queer people, it's very hard to have to build our own family and to have our own kids. It takes a lot of money and a lot of effort," he said. "This is a way to contribute and enrich our lives at the same time."

World.title: One of Calgary's most decorated Second World War veterans dies at 101
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of Calgary's most decorated Second World War veterans and a leader in the city's naval and military community has died at the age of 101.

Born in Winnipeg on Nov. 5, 1924, navy Capt. William (Bill) Wilson enlisted in the Royal Canadian Navy in 1942, serving aboard HMCS Ottawa as a seaman gunner during the latter stages of the Battle of the Atlantic and taking part in the D-Day landings at Normandy.

"He started off in sea cadets in Winnipeg, and he was very, very keen to be able to join the war," Scott Hausberg, who knew Wilson well, told CBC Radio's The Homestretch Tuesday.

Hausberg said as soon as Wilson turned 18 he was at the recruiting office, but after undergoing the necessary tests he was told he had failed his medical exam because he was underweight.

"So, the clerk said, 'There's a store across the street. Go over there, buy a bunch of bananas, eat them all, come back, and we'll weigh you again,'" said Hausberg, who is also the president of the Naval Museum of Alberta Society.

"So he did that and he came back and he gained enough ounces, I guess, to pass the medical and that's how he got in the navy."

William (Bill) Wilson smiles in this undated handout photo. (The Canadian Press/Handout - Facebook, @CanadaRemembers, Veterans Affairs Canada)

In a 2015 video for Valour Canada, a non-profit for Canadian military history, Wilson said he and his unit "had no idea" about the magnitude of D-Day, code-named Operation Overlord.

"We really weren't quite sure what we were going to see," he said.

There on Normandy's shores, the largest land, sea and air invasion in history — made up of almost 160,000 Allied troops and some 14,000 Canadians — took German defences by surprise.

The invasion is now remembered as the beginning of the end of the Second World War.

Amid the dark, choking smoke and "bloody noisy" gunfire, Wilson said sailor after sailor shot out from landing craft with their eyes on the beaches.

LISTEN | Remembering Captain Bill Wilson: The Homestretch 8:01 Remembering Captain Bill Wilson One of the leaders in Calgary's naval community and one of our city's most decorated veterans, has died at the age of 101. We speak with someone who knew him well to look back on his life.

Many were quickly cut down by bullets.

"You can't visualize guys coming out of a barge and meeting machine-gun fire and mortars and shells from artillery," he said. "We couldn't visualize that."

In all, 4,414 Allied troops, including 381 Canadians, were killed that day. And at the end of the 77-day Battle of Normandy, 73,000 Allied forces were killed and 153,000 wounded.

"I think [D-Day] was the best day of the war for the world," Wilson told Valour Canada. "We did free all of Europe, and Canada was there. For a little nation like ours, it still amazes me."

'Everything he did was in service to Canada'

According to a 2013 Alberta government profile , published when Wilson was inducted into the Alberta Order of Excellence, upon his return to Canada, he worked for Canadian Pacific in Winnipeg, before eventually moving to Calgary in the 1970s.

Following the war, he joined the naval reserve and retired from active service in 1979.

Wilson was also a founding member of the Naval Museum of Alberta in 1984 — along with Commodore Laraine Orthlieb — where he was a "driving force" in fundraising for the museum's original building and acquiring many of its artifacts, said Hausberg.

"He was one of those people where you couldn't say no to him."

WATCH | Capt. Bill Wilson describes his experience during the D-Day landings:

"When he found out that there was a three-inch/70[-caliber] gun sitting along the shore in Esquimalt, British Columbia, and the museum needed it, he'd go and call the admiral and said, 'I want that gun,'" Hausberg said.

"He got a lot of art artifacts into our museum. That's why it is the largest naval museum in the country."

Hausberg said Wilson's ability to acquire any artifact from anywhere earned him the nickname "Captain Rabbit," a naval term for acquiring something by any means.

In 2001, he served as the general manager of a campaign that successfully raised $26 million needed to open The Military Museums — the largest complex of its kind in Canada — combining the pre-existing Museum of the Regiments with the naval museum and a new air force museum.

In light of his many accomplishments, Hausberg said Wilson's greatest legacy is the steady example he set through his commitment to serving the community and country.

"Everything that he did was in service to Canada, and he deserves to be remembered for that."

A celebration of life will be held Aug. 10 at 2 p.m. at Calgary's HMCS Tecumseh, the Naval Reserve unit where he most recently served.

World.title: A concert to remember: Metal band rocks out at Ottawa hospital, granting patient's wish
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa's Bruyère Health hosted a high-energy hard rock concert to help one longtime patient live out his dream of attending a heavy metal show. The CBC's Jenna Legge reports.

Hospitals aren't the usual venue for a high-energy hard rock concert, but that's exactly what took place at Ottawa's Bruyère Health last week, helping one longtime patient live out his dream of attending a heavy metal show.

With a colourful light show, hair-blowing fans and aggressive headbanging, a board room at the hospital was transformed into a rock club last Tuesday after 27-year-old Tim Berry expressed his wish to rock out there.

Roshene Lawson, a clinical chaplain at Bruyère Health, said she was visiting Berry after he'd received some bad health news and was dwelling on the things he'd missed out on.

"I said, 'Well, we can talk about all the stuff you've lost, or we can talk about how you want to live for however much longer you're around," Lawson said.

The Scepter performs for patients at Bruyère Health on July 21. (Bruyère Health)

What Berry wanted was to attend a heavy metal show. Lawson called Scott McClinton, owner of hard rock venue the Dominion Tavern in the ByWard Market, who in turn recruited local band The Scepter.

"It was a quick yes, and then he reached out to The Scepter, and they gave a quick yes," Lawson told CBC’s All In A Day. "All of a sudden, people in heavy metal outfits with guitars and stuff are asking where the chaplain is."

Berry's condition was deemed too fragile to leave the hospital, so the crew decided to bring the show to him. With Berry’s approval, it turned into a full-blown event for patients at Bruyère Health on July 21, coming together within a week.

Heavy metal band The Scepter quickly accepted the invitation to put on a show at Bruyère Health. (Bruyère Health)

"He had tears and I joked with him, I said, 'Are the tears because it's so bloody loud?'" Lawson said. "And he laughed and he said, ‘No, I'm happy'"

Lawson said even the "tough heavy metal guys" had tears in their eyes, too.

"It was absolutely emotional," McClinton recalled. "I never thought I'd cry during a metal show, but that definitely happened."

11:36 A heavy metal concert in a hospital? When a patient shared with staff at Bruyère Health that it was his dream to see a heavy metal concert, they made it happen. Dominion Tavern and local metal band The Scepter came through to deliver an electric performance for patients at Bruyère.

The Scepter pulled out all the stops, making the most of the unconventional venue by using the space between each patient as a catwalk to show off their guitar-shredding skills.

"We had enough space with all the lights and stuff to still move around and go up to the patients and give them a little taste of our heavy metal might," said guitarist Josh Collins.

After the show, Berry met with the band and got some merch including a T-shirt and CD.

Chaplain Roshene Lawson says it is important to think outside the box when it comes to patient care. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

Lawson said it was much more than a fun musical experience: It was about providing the best quality of life for a patient she helps navigate the ups and downs of hospital life.

"I listened to what it was that would bring him meaning and value. It's not my role to judge that," she said. "It's my role to support and listen."

She said while a strong focus on medical care is crucial, the clinical team at Bruyère Health also prioritizes spiritual wellness.

"Sometimes we've got to think outside the box, and in this case I went to a heavy metal concert."

World.title: Canada, allies express renewed concern over North Korean IT worker scheme
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada and multiple allies released an alert on Friday detailing a North Korean scheme to fund its weapons of mass destruction program.

According to the joint statement released by Global Affairs Canada (GAC) and its counterparts in Japan, the U.S., the U.K. and a half-dozen other countries, North Korea has continuously deployed a network of remote IT workers to defraud businesses and transfer revenues toward the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

The individuals within the network impersonate workers from other countries to obtain work and income with private companies, then remit their salaries to their parent North Korean agencies, the statement said.

Those funds are then used to expand North Korea's nuclear weapons arsenal, according to the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), an independent, intergovernmental anti-money laundering and counterterrorist financing watchdog.

The FATF has put North Korea on its "black list" as a high-risk jurisdiction, meaning the organization calls on all countries to deploy such countermeasures as terminating relationships with North Korean banks and limiting business relationships and transactions with North Korean nationals.

WATCH | North Korea shows off new missiles: North Korea flaunts new missiles in military parade | Duration 0:34 North Korean leader Kim Jong-un unveiled a new intercontinental ballistic missile at a massive military parade marking 80 years of the ruling party.

Following a 2017 United Nations resolution , all member countries are required to repatriate any North Korean nationals earning income within their borders back to North Korea, with few exceptions.

Canada, along with France, Germany, Italy, Japan, South Korea, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S., urged countries and companies to better understand North Korea's scheme and to deploy effective countermeasures against the illicit network.

It's not the first time Canada has issued an advisory about the risks posed by North Korea's IT worker scheme.

"Our countries have repeatedly issued information to warn the international community and private sector of the threat posed by North Korean IT workers," the joint statement reads. "We continue to actively monitor and counter the North Korean IT worker threat."

How does the scheme work?

The North Korean workers deployed to carry out the regime's plot are typically highly skilled in IT-related work and look for jobs and contracts in areas like web page development, mobile applications, software and blockchain applications, the statement says.

They often obtain work in foreign countries by falsifying their nationality or identity through a few common methods.

The scheme is also "increasingly likely" to involve proxy agents from third countries, according to the alert.

That might mean using their identification documents to forge online accounts, but it can go so far as to have the proxy participate in job interviews and establish in-person contact to create a false sense of trust with the company.

GAC and its counterparts said the workers in the network generally reside in North Korea, China and Russia, as well as in Southeast Asian and African countries, using third-party proxies, VPNs and other tools to conceal the fact they are working from abroad.

The schemes may also involve "laptop farms," which make use of company-provided laptops that are then accessed remotely by North Korean IT workers to cover their true location.

A TV screen shows an image of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un during a news program airing at a railway station in Seoul, South Korea, on Feb. 26. (Ahn Young-joon/The Associated Press)

Identifying a North Korean agent

GAC and its counterparts provided a list of behaviours and characteristics often exhibited by workers involved in North Korean IT schemes.

They suggested web companies keep an eye out for certain behaviour, including frequent changes to registered information like account and banking details; multiple accounts created using the same identification document and accessed from the same IP address; a single account accessed from multiple IP addresses within a short period of time; and an account remains logged in for an unusually long period of time.

For companies hiring, some of the flagged behaviours include refusing to participate in video calls; video call discrepancies like photo ID mismatches or video feeds that seem manipulated or artificially generated; requesting payments in cryptocurrency; and signs the account is being operated by multiple people.

GAC and its counterparts said if multiple behaviours relate to someone applying for work, it's possibly a North Korean IT worker fraudulently seeking employment.

"North Korean IT workers often operate in teams, and the individual whom a hiring or procuring official interacts with may change depending on the time of day," the statement reads.

Big payouts toward North Korean weapons

According to the U.S. Treasury Department, North Korean IT worker schemes defrauded American businesses and generated $800 million US in 2024.

In April, two Americans were sentenced to prison for participating a plot that generated $5 million. Typical of the scheme, it involved a laptop farm operated by the two Americans, accessed remotely by a team of North Korean workers to extract income.

In that particular case, North Korean IT workers made use of at least 80 stolen U.S. identities to fraudulently obtain work at more than 100 American companies.

By generating funds through a network of illicit workers extracting income from companies globally, North Korea continues to finance its proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, according to the statement.

In March, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un promised to expand the regime's nuclear arsenal , and just last month his sister, Kim Yo-jong, said North Korea will never back down from its status as a country militarized by nuclear weapons.

World.title: What is Ceuta, and how was the Spanish enclave near Morocco breached by 60,000 migrants?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Authorities have described it as "absolute chaos," "unsustainable" and "a violation."

At least 57 people have died after tens of thousands of migrants breached the Moroccan border into Spain's Ceuta enclave by land and sea, causing shock and division in Europe.

Current estimates are some 60,000 people crossed into the Spanish enclave in North Africa on Thursday — and by Friday evening, that a n estimated 48,300 had returned to Morocco.

Many had arrived by sea, by swimming the five kilometres f rom the Moroccan town of Fnideq. Others attempted to cross from the nearby town of Belyounech, which is a shorter distance.

"It took me two hours," a swimmer in a wetsuit told France 24, the French public broadcaster.

"It was very tough," said another swimmer.

Some of those who crossed appeared to be children and unaccompanied minors, prompting a warning from a Moroccan NGO that taking children on irregular migration journeys puts their lives in danger.

WATCH | Spain deploys military after thousands enter Ceuta: Spain deploys military after thousands of migrants enter Ceuta | Duration 2:03 Spain deployed troops to reinforce police after thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in North Africa. The scene was reminiscent of 2021, when about 10,000 migrants entered the territory.

Spanish authorities said 57 bodies had been recovered on the Spanish side of the border and that there could be additional casualties on the Moroccan side. They said some drowned and some were crushed while trying to climb the breakwater that holds the border fence.

A Moroccan that Agence France-Presse only identified by his first name, Abdelhakim, said he walked 14 kilometres to reach the Morocco-Spain border, then attempted to cross by sea.

"I found myself completely submerged and saw two men die right before my eyes," he told the news agency. "That's when I backed away and remembered that I have two children of my own, and that I couldn't risk my life."

Here's what we know so far about what happened, and why.

What is Ceuta?

Ceuta and the larger Spanish territory of Melilla, which is some 400 kilometres east, are located on the northern shores of the Mediterranean coast at the tip of Africa. Both autonomous cities belong to Spain and share the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.

Both also periodically experience surges in attempted crossings by migrants seeking to reach ​Europe, but the scale of Thursday's rush appeared unprecedented.

The city of Ceuta is an 18.5-square-kilometre peninsula with a population of about 83,000 people (so, when 60,000 crossed the border in a day, the population surged by 73 per cent). It's separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.

In Spanish possession since 1580, Ceuta is home to a mixed population of Christians and Muslims, and Spanish and Moroccan residents and day workers.

Morocco does not officially recognize Ceuta and Melilla as Spanish territory, and often refers to them as occupied lands.

Why is it a migrant destination?

Spain is a main point of arrival into Europe for migrants seeking better economic opportunities or an escape from violence in their home countries.

Ceuta and Melilla are heavily fortified, as the territories are seen as a destination for those trying to reach Spain from Morocco and other parts of Africa. Typically, many migrants who reach Ceuta or Melilla are immediately turned back, while others held in migrant shelters are processed and can apply for asylum in Spain.

As NPR noted even back in 2014, "African migrants keep arriving by land and sea — straining public services — to reach an African city with European health care." Many of those interviewed on Thursday told various media outlets they had come to Ceuta in hopes of finding work.

Moroccan Fatima Zahra told AFP she'd attempted the crossing because she wanted to try her luck with a better job, adding she works "under appalling conditions."

"Migration is about improving our lives. We agreed we would try the idea of crossing and trust in Allah," Ayoub El Abyad told Reuters, after completing the journey by hitching rides with two drivers.

PHOTOS | Thousands cross into Ceuta:

Why the rush Thursday?

It's not immediately clear what caused the rush for the border, although authorities in Ceuta and Madrid have linked it to a recent decision by the Spanish Supreme Court that ruled migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported, unlike those who cross by land or climb the border fence.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez blamed human smugglers.

"It appears that this interpretation of the Supreme Court’s ruling spread like wildfire over the past few hours through the networks of human trafficking organizations, triggering the kind of mass surge we witnessed yesterday," Sánchez said.

That said, s ome activists in Morocco argued that most migrants would have been unaware of such a legal decision.

According to Spanish broadcaster RTVE, the ruling spread on social media on Thursday, which reportedly encouraged people to try to enter Spain by swimming to Ceuta. Hespress, an English-language Moroccan news site, reports that a public Facebook group with 20,000 members shared maps, tips and even where to get diving fins to help with the crossing.

But AFP says it may have started with rumours of a rare border opening.

"I woke up in the morning and heard that Ceuta had opened," Fatima Zahra told AFP.

"Suddenly they heard that the borders were open and that some young people had crossed, so everyone ended up here," said another Moroccan named Karim.

According to local media in Morocco, videos circulating online show people carrying elderly family members on their backs, or their babies into the sea.

What else could be behind sudden surge?

As Reuters points out, while the surge was sudden, it was also years in the making.

In Morocco, where deep-seated anger toward poor public services and rampant poverty spilled over into major protests last year, many young people spend years waiting for a chance to cross the border in search of better prospects.

Migrants from Morocco arrive at the Spanish border in Ceuta on July 31, 2026. (Fabian Bimmer/Reuters)

A quarter of Moroccans aged 15 to 24 are not in education, employment or training, official data shows.

Calm seas at this time of year make swimming a more feasible option for migrants, Mauricio Valiente, director of Spanish refugee charity CEAR, told Reuters.

In a post on X, Spain's civil police association said there had been too few officers in place to monitor the fence during the surge on Thursday, making them unable to stop the rush.

Meanwhile, Matteo Villa, a migration researcher at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, told the Guardian that politics was most likely involved, noting that a recent trip by the Spanish prime minister to Algiers likely angered a lot of Moroccans.

Villa said it's possible Morocco may have loosened the border to show it has "the upper hand."

"The events ... serve as an unmistakable stress test for Mediterranean power dynamics," Amine Ayoub, a fellow at the Middle East Forum who lives in Morocco, wrote in Ynet News.

WATCH | 'Absolute chaos': 'Absolute chaos': Spain to deploy military after thousands of migrants enter Ceuta enclave | Duration 3:34 The Spanish government has said it will deploy its military to restore order at its border with Morocco in Ceuta after thousands of migrants streamed into the small Spanish territory. The head of Ceuta's Civil Guard union described the sudden border breach as "absolute chaos," adding that the border has "totally collapsed."

What was the response?

Spain deployed its armed forces and additional police to restore order in Ceuta. Spanish authorities said they would try to expel those who had entered illegally as quickly as possible.

On the Moroccan side of the border, security forces beat back crowds with batons and tear gas at the gates to Ceuta, trying to prevent more from storming across. Migrants from Morocco also attempted to cross into Melilla, where they clashed with police.

By Friday afternoon, most migrants were trying to leave Ceuta.

Migrants walk toward the border with Morocco to leave Ceuta, Spain, on July 31. (Fabian Bimmer/Reuters)

Why did so many go back to Morocco?

Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers' association representing Civil Guard officers, told the Associated Press that thousands of migrants, including unaccompanied children, were left sleeping in parks and on sidewalks, while others roamed the streets aimlessly.

Several hundred people could be seen returning to Morocco through border posts and holes in the fence, with some saying they could not find food or shelter in Ceuta.

Moroccan media reported that several people who returned have shared videos online describing two days without water and have to sleep outside. Some returnees have also reportedly said they expected to keep going to mainland Spain, but instead found themselves stuck.

"Honestly, I don't even know why I came. And now I'm going back," a young Moroccan man, who said he was from Tangier, told Reuters.

"There was no food inside Ceuta and we were kicked out badly by the [Spanish] army," said another returnee identified as Ayman, 20, a hairdresser.

That said, multiple media outlets reported that migrants were still trying to enter Ceuta on Friday by swimming around the breakwater.

World.title: 'Our house would shake': Shania Twain opens up about growing up in 'violent' home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For a young Shania Twain, home wasn't always a safe place.

Long before she became a global country music superstar, the Man! I Feel Like a Woman! singer, 60, says she spent her childhood in Timmins, Ont., growing up in what she describes as a "very violent" home, caught up in a chaotic cycle fuelled by her mother and stepfather's "volatile relationship."

"They loved each other. They went through so many ups and downs together, but they fought a lot, and they got violent often," Twain revealed on Thursday's episode of NPR's Wild Card with Rachel Martin.

When Martin asked whether she ever got caught in the crossfire of that violence, the five-time Grammy winner replied, "Yeah, with me, too."

"If I was standing in the wrong place at the wrong time, definitely."

Twain, who was born Eilleen Edwards, added that both of her parents were "pretty harsh physically" and that she and her sisters, Jill and Carrie Ann, "definitely got smacked around a lot."

"And kicked around, sometimes literally kicked around."

Still, Twain said it was her parents, Sharon and Jerry Twain, who "hurt each other the most."

"My mom, she would lose clumps of hair, she was bruised often in the face and … it was pretty bad sometimes. Our house would shake. Those walls would shake," Twain recalled, adding that it was "very traumatic."

"It gets loud and scary, like a really bad thunderstorm."

WATCH | Shania Twain on her 'traumatic' childhood:

Twain's mother, Sharon Edwards, divorced her biological father, Clarence Edwards, when the future country music icon was two. She later married Jerry Twain who adopted Shania and her sisters.

Twain said the family grew up poor, often rationing food, and surviving on "stale bread." She says her mother and step father's financial struggles frequently became the source of their fights.

"They would argue over … 'Can't pay the bills. Now we're gonna run out of heat, and now, who's fault is that?'" Twain said.

Twain says her mother tried to leave her stepfather several times, particularly when the violence would reach "its peak" and the "neighbours would call the cops." But they never managed to break completely loose.

"My mother did often try to leave. She did leave — we did leave — but you know, he'd always find us or she'd always give in and go back," Twain said. "It was a cycle."

The couple ended up remaining together until they were both killed in a car accident in 1987 when Twain was 22.

It's not the first time the country singer has spoken publicly about her turbulent upbringing.

The You're Still the One singer opened up about her childhood in her 2011 memoir From This Moment On, where she shared how her stepfather physically, emotionally and sexually abused her for years while she also witnessed him repeatedly assault her mother.

World.title: What you need to know about FIFA's private investment plan — and the backlash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Senior FIFA adviser Carlos Cordeiro has resigned in protest over the organization's proposal to sell a stake in the World Cup. Cordeiro called the plan 'a bad deal for football' following UEFA's official vote to boycott future FIFA tournaments if the proposal proceeds.

Less than two weeks since the conclusion of the 2026 World Cup, soccer is once again front-page news thanks to a new proposal by FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

Not one to shy away from big announcements, Infantino caught many in the soccer world unaware with a plan to sell off part of FIFA's commercial interests to private investors.

It's caused significant backlash in the soccer world, including the prospect of European nations boycotting future editions of the World Cup — and on Friday, the resignation of Infantino's key adviser Carlos Cordeiro, who called the plan "a bad deal for football."

Here's what you need to know.

WATCH | FIFA's World Cup profits soar: How FIFA got even richer this World Cup | Duration 2:24 CBC’s Jonathon Gatehouse breaks down how Gianni Infantino doubled profits for the 2026 World Cup, and how much of that money ends up in the hands of organizations like Soccer Canada.

What are FIFA, UEFA and the other soccer confederations?

The Fédération Internationale de Football Association is the international governing body of association football, also known as soccer. Founded in 1904 and headquartered in Switzerland, FIFA today has many stated objectives , including overseeing the development and innovation in the sport, conducting disciplinary matters and organizing international tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cup.

FIFA's membership is currently comprised of 211 national soccer federations (such as Canada Soccer), which are the effective owners of FIFA as a non-profit association under Swiss law.

Each national federation is also a member of six continental confederations that oversee the sport in their respective regions:

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol (CONMEBOL).

Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF).

Oceania Football Confederation (OFC).

Union of European Football Associations (UEFA).

UEFA is arguably the most powerful of the six, as it counts many of the sport's most successful countries among its 55 members — including France, Germany, Italy and current world champion Spain — as well as the four "home nations" of the United Kingdom, where the sport was formalized.

Infantino, left, stands with Spanish Football Association president Rafael Louzán after the trophy ceremony for the World Cup final on July 19. Spain would be one of the nations involved in a UEFA boycott. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

What is the FIFA plan causing the latest furor?

On Tuesday, FIFA president Gianni Infantino announced plans to form a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) that would run competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup.

Under FIFA's plan, which was pitched as a way to boost the development of soccer around the world, 20 per cent of FFE would be sold off to private investors, including a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, brother of U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

National federations that approve FFE would see their promised $8 million US development funds from FIFA more than doubled to $20 million US for the next four years. It would then increase to $22 million US and $24 million US in the following cycles through 2038, FIFA said.

What was UEFA's reaction?

The continental confederations appear to have been blindsided by Infantino's announcement.

Almost immediately, UEFA called an emergency meeting of its member federations. On Thursday, it released a strongly worded statement saying its members would boycott all the global soccer body's competitions as long as the FEE proposal remains on the table.

UEFA delivered a stinging rebuke of Infantino's plan, saying "the World Cup is not for sale."

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors."

It added that FIFA's plan, under which "commercial return becomes a permanent obligation" and "investor expectations become a daily pressure," would upend the way soccer is governed.

"You're giving undue influence to people that are not going to necessarily be motivated by what's best for soccer but what's best for their bank accounts," said Moshe Lander, a sports economist at Concordia University in Montreal.

Spanish players celebrate after winning the 2023 Women's World Cup at the final in Sydney, Australia. The next Women's World Cup is scheduled to be hosted in Brazil in summer 2027. (Hannah Mckay/Reuters)

Which competitions would be affected by a boycott?

Three FIFA World Cup tournaments are still to be played this year:

The U-20 Women's World Cup in Poland is set to kick off on Sept. 5.

The U-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco is due to get underway on Oct. 17.

The U-17 Men's World Cup in Qatar gets underway in mid-November.

The next senior World Cup, the women's tournament, is scheduled for next summer in Brazil.

UEFA has sent a "powerful message" in threatening to boycott future FIFA events, said Graham Scott, a former English Premier League referee and now a correspondent with The Athletic.

"The withdrawal of UEFA countries from any FIFA tournament effectively renders it worthless," he said.

What about the other confederations?

The confederations covering Asia, and North and Central America and the Caribbean have also come out against the FFE proposal.

While neither went as far as declaring a boycott, both the AFC and CONCACAF shared UEFA's alarm over FIFA's lack of consultation with its members.

On Friday, a statement by the AFC raised concerns over the divisions the plan had caused, saying "any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the [World Cup] must be reconsidered."

The Asian confederation said it's not the first time FIFA has put together a proposal with no input from members, adding that the association must "undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework."

The statement was released after AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa sent a letter to member federations Wednesday saying, "FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football," and warning of risks to their own competitions.

Several hours after UEFA's statement was released Thursday, CONCACAF said its member federations, which include Canada, had rejected the proposal to create FFE.

A statement called for "greater transparency and proper governance" and raised concerns about "the lack of due process surrounding the proposal."

CONCACAF also questioned why FIFA deemed that private equity was necessary after what was the most profitable World Cup in history.

The CAF says it will discuss the proposal at a meeting next week, while the OFC said it had begun a consultation process with its members about the proposal. As of Friday afternoon, CONMEBOL, which covers South America, had not released a statement about the proposal.

The combined votes of the AFC, CONCACAF and UEFA would be enough to defeat the FFE proposal, which requires a majority from member federations to pass.

U.S. President Donald Trump, left, and Infantino stand together during the trophy presentation after the final of the FIFA World Cup 2026, the most lucrative in the tournament's history. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

Has Infantino put his position in jeopardy?

Prior to the FFE announcement, it looked as if Infantino would easily win re-election for a fourth term as FIFA president when a vote of member federations is held next March.

That's perhaps less of a certainty now, especially considering the AFC's opposition to FFE and the comments from its president Sheikh Salman, who has been a staunch ally of Infantino.

It also follows concern in the soccer world over some aspects of the recent World Cup hosted by Canada, Mexico and the U.S., including the high price of tickets, controversies over the video assistant referee, the introduction of hydration breaks during games, and a red card for an American player that was rescinded after the intervention of U.S. President Donald Trump.

FIFA has set a Nov. 18 deadline for potential candidates to declare in the vote for the association's next president.
