We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and kindergartens in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and kindergartens will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to kindergartens. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. It is working on tools that would require platforms to verify the age of users https://t.co/G7qeEl2q9x — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. The missile entered Poland during a period of intensive overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, travelling around 100 km over Polish territory before exploding in a field in the Lublin region on Thursday morning. Nie miejmy żadnych złudzeń. Tego typu sytuacje albo tego typu prowokacje będą się zdarzać – powiedział wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk w @faktypofaktach, komentując wybuch rakiety na Lubelszczyźnie.https://t.co/IKxuGNwe05 — tvn24 (@tvn24) July 30, 2026 “We can confidently confirm that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile, a cruise missile capable of carrying even nuclear warheads, which exploded on impact,” deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk told broadcaster TVN24 late on Thursday. The object was “a potentially very dangerous missile,” Tomczyk added. Asked whether the incident could have been a deliberate move by Moscow, he said that no possibilities could be ruled out. “We don’t know, and if we do find out, it will mainly be through intelligence. I’m sure the coming weeks will provide us with more answers,” the deputy minister said. Tomczyk said Poland was working closely with Ukraine, adding that 20 of the roughly 70 missiles fired by Russia overnight from Wednesday to Thursday were at one point heading towards Poland. “It is also worth noting that the vast majority of these missiles were shot down by Ukraine over Ukrainian territory, which clearly bore the full brunt of the attack,” he said. He added that a Ukrainian pilot had tracked the missile that later fell on Polish territory but was unable to intercept it. “He turned back 20 seconds before reaching the border,” Tomczyk said, adding that the pilot “could not have flown into” Polish airspace. An object crashed into a field 100 km from Poland’s border with Ukraine overnight after a major Russian attack. Ukrainian officials said it was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while Poland reported an "extremely difficult night for our air defence"https://t.co/QIpRQfej5S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2026 Prosecutors who concluded their work at the site on Thursday said the missile contained a “significant amount of explosive material”. Investigators collected fragments and soil samples from the impact site, where the explosion left a crater around 10 metres wide and 5 metres deep. “The crater has been filled and the site handed back to its owner. The Territorial Defence Force combed through an area of approximately 3 km² and found numerous rocket debris, including propulsion components,” the Lublin prosecutor’s office said. Following the latest incident, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the government would, paradoxically, consider providing Ukraine with further military aid, including additional Patriot air-defence systems if necessary. “Our intention is to ensure that Ukraine does not lose this war,” Tusk said. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will deport a Colombian citizen who performed a Nazi salute during his visit to the former German-Nazi death camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. Kolumbii 🇨🇴, który na terenie Muzeum Auschwitz-Birkenau propagował nazizm i znieważył miejsce pamięci. Komendant #PlacówkaSGwKrakowie wydał wobec cudzoziemca decyzję o zobowiązaniu do powrotu oraz 5-letni zakaz wjazdu do 🇵🇱 i państw strefy Schengen. pic.twitter.com/kzfw1Kzw8w — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) July 30, 2026 Police in Oświęcim, the town where the museum is located, said in mid-July that they had detained a man after being notified by museum guards of a possible offence. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Polish prosecutors have indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz, which he then published in an online video Denying Nazi crimes carries a prison sentence of up to three years in Poland https://t.co/WCSm7O4gAx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 4, 2026 The Auschwitz Museum has in recent years dealt with various cases of visitors misbehaving, including in ways that are punishable by law. Earlier this month, prosecutors in Poland indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz. In 2025, an Israeli teenager who was seen doing a fascist salute at the former German-Nazi camp was fined for propagating Nazism. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. The growth has coincided with the international expansion of its firms, more foreign investments, and a rapidly expanding tourism sector. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped improve Poland’s visibility. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. TYLKO U NAS! Wybuch i ogromny krater na #Lubelszczyźnie. Mamy zdjęcia! >> https://t.co/BrX7XneP7F Fot. Ukraine has offered Poland assistance in investigating the scene, he added. Earlier in the morning, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ) said that air defence radars had detected at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine overnight whose trajectories could have posed a potential threat to Polish airspace. An unidentified object was detected in Polish airspace at 3:40 a.m. travelling westward, DORSZ said. An F-16 fighter jet was dispatched to identify and intercept it. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. Zwołałem w związku z tym zespół koordynacyjny z udziałem Ministra Obrony i odpowiednich służb, które od wielu godzin pracują na miejscu zdarzenia i… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 30, 2026 Tusk said the initial information suggested the object was likely a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, echoing earlier comments made by Ukraine’s acting foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, but stressed that investigators would need to establish the precise type and origin of the object. “We will want to be 100% certain: what kind of missile, who launched it, whether it was the explosion of the payload or the impact of the missile itself that caused this crater,” he said at a press conference in Lublin. The prime minister added that Polish forces had been prepared to shoot down the object had it continued flying in a way that posed a threat. Tusk added that another missile approached the Polish border but did not enter Polish airspace. “This initial information clearly indicates that the relevant services, the military, our pilots, and our aircraft acted very quickly and efficiently. There was no immediate threat due to the missile falling in an undeveloped area,” Tusk said. He added that he had discussed the incident with opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. Niezwykle ciężka noc dla naszej obrony powietrznej, systemów obserwacji i wykrywania zagrożeń. Dziękuję gen. I. Later, speaking alongside Tusk, he said Polish F-16 fighter jets had been operating near the Polish-Ukrainian border since about 2 a.m. “In addition, reconnaissance aircraft operating over Polish airspace and allied aircraft for aerial refuelling, which took off from Germany, have been activated,” he said. An early warning system was activated in Lublin and several other areas of the province because of Russian air attacks on Ukraine. The alarm lasted about 13 minutes, according to the interior minister. The opposition criticised the authorities for not providing residents with further information about the reason for the alarm. “A few minutes of alarm, no information in the mainstream media about what was happening, some residents didn’t even hear the sirens, and no text messages with an alert from the Government Centre for Security (RCB),” wrote Michał Dworczyk, a Law and Justice (PiS) MP, on social media. In 2022, a stray missile struck the Polish village of Przewodów, killing two people. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. World.title: Budapest landmarks to go dark: Parliament, Buda Castle and Citadella lights switched off
World.content:
Several of Budapest’s best-known landmarks will temporarily go dark as Hungary introduces further energy-saving measures in response to the country’s critical electricity situation.

Officials announced on Friday that the decorative lighting of the Hungarian Parliament will be switched off, while the illumination of buildings in the Buda Castle District will be gradually turned off by Monday.

The measures come as the government prepares for the expected shutdown of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, which has been forced to reduce output because of historically low water levels in the Danube.

Parliament joins nationwide energy-saving effort

In a Facebook post, Deputy Speaker Anikó Hallerné Nagy, who is currently performing the duties of Speaker of Parliament, said the National Assembly would also contribute to national energy-saving efforts.

She said Parliament would place even greater emphasis on conscious and efficient energy use, with switching off the building’s decorative lighting forming part of those efforts.

Buda Castle, Carmelite Monastery and Citadella also affected

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced that the decorative lighting of buildings managed by the Castle Administration would also be switched off gradually by Monday. According to the minister, the lights will remain off until operating them no longer places an unnecessary burden on Hungary’s electricity grid.

The measure will affect several prominent landmarks, including:

the Buda Castle complex,

the Carmelite Monastery,

the Ministry of Social Affairs and Family building,

and the Citadella.

Vitézy said reducing all non-essential electricity consumption is justified while the country’s power system faces exceptional pressure.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Part of wider emergency measures

The lighting shutdown is one of a series of steps announced as Hungary braces for a challenging period in its electricity supply. Government officials have urged businesses, public institutions and households to reduce electricity consumption, particularly during the daily peak period between 5 PM and 10 PM, as the country prepares for the potential temporary shutdown of the Paks nuclear plant.

World.title: Budapest smashes 105-year heat record as brutal heatwave tightens grip on Hungary
World.content:
Budapest has set a new daily heat record after temperatures climbed to 39.4°C in the capital’s Újpest district on Friday afternoon, according to preliminary data from Hungary’s national meteorological service, HungaroMet.

The new record is 2°C higher than the previous Budapest record for 31 July, which stood at 37.4°C and had remained unbeaten since 1921, when it was measured at Gellért Hill and Törökvész.

National record matched, but not broken

While the national daily heat record survived, it was equalled at two locations. Both the Újpest weather station and the Győr-Likócs station recorded 39.4°C, matching the long-standing national record for 31 July, originally measured in Szerep in 1917. HungaroMet noted that the figures are still preliminary and will be officially confirmed after validation.

Hungary braces for even more extreme temperatures

The record comes as Hungary experiences one of its most intense heatwaves in recent years. Friday’s daytime highs ranged between 34°C and 39°C across much of the country. The extreme weather is expected to continue. Forecasts indicate temperatures of 35–40°C over the weekend, with some areas potentially reaching 41–42°C early next week if current weather models prove accurate.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

A third-degree heat alert remains in force until midnight on 4 August, with authorities continuing to urge residents to stay hydrated, avoid strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day, and check on elderly relatives and neighbours. Meteorologists currently expect the exceptional heat to persist until at least 7 August, although longer-range forecasts may still change.

World.title: Hungarian government announces one of the country’s largest renewable energy investment programmes in decades
World.content:
The Hungarian government has announced one of the country’s largest renewable energy investment programmes in decades, unveiling plans to dramatically expand wind power, electricity storage and grid infrastructure as it responds to the ongoing energy crisis triggered by the Danube’s record-low water level.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar presented the plans on Friday during a press conference at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, where officials continue to prepare for a possible temporary shutdown of the facility because of the prolonged drought.

Government plans 4 GW of new wind power

Magyar announced that the government has approved plans to develop 4 gigawatts (GW) of new wind power capacity by 2030, roughly double the installed capacity of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

According to the prime minister, the projects will be financed with private investment, while a public consultation on proposed locations for the new wind farms will begin shortly.

He said the previous government had effectively blocked wind farm development for years, adding that the current administration intends to accelerate permitting procedures through a new regulatory framework and the use of European Union funding.

Billions to modernise Hungary’s electricity grid

The renewable energy expansion will be accompanied by a major upgrade of Hungary’s electricity network.

Magyar said an HUF 868 billion energy development programme is already under way, while a EUR 1.5 billion scheme financed through Hungary’s recovered EU Recovery and Resilience Facility funds will support improvements to the national electricity grid.

Applications for those projects are due to close at the end of next month. The aim, he said, is to ensure the power network can continue operating reliably even under extreme weather conditions.

Large-scale battery storage also planned

Alongside expanding renewable generation, the government plans to build 3 GW of electricity storage capacity by 2030.

According to Magyar, increasing battery storage will make it easier to integrate renewable electricity into the national grid while strengthening Hungary’s long-term energy resilience.

“We must ensure that Hungary’s energy supply becomes as independent as possible from both Russian energy and the water level of the Danube,” the prime minister said.

Budapest Airport joins national energy-saving effort

Meanwhile, Budapest Airport announced that it will voluntarily reduce electricity consumption over the next 10 days in response to pressure on Hungary’s power system. The airport said the measures will focus on reducing non-essential energy use, particularly during the daily peak demand period between 5 PM and 10 PM, while maintaining safe and uninterrupted airport operations.

Passengers using Terminal 2 may notice slightly warmer indoor temperatures during those hours, as air conditioning will operate at a reduced level. The airport added that it remains in close contact with electricity providers and relevant authorities while encouraging employees and business partners to conserve energy wherever possible.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Shift towards greater energy independence

The announcements come as Hungary faces mounting pressure on its electricity system due to the possible temporary shutdown of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, which has reduced output because of the Danube’s exceptionally low water level.

The government says expanding renewable energy, modernising the electricity grid and investing in large-scale storage are central to reducing Hungary’s dependence on imported energy and making the country’s power system more resilient to future climate-related challenges.

World.title: PM Magyar says Hungary enters ‘one of the worst energy crises in decades’, shares new Paks shutdown date
World.content:
Hungary is entering what Prime Minister Péter Magyar has described as one of the country’s most serious energy crises in decades, with the most critical period expected to begin on Monday as the Paks Nuclear Power Plant moves closer to a possible full shutdown.

Speaking at two emergency press briefings on Friday (first at MOL’s Danube Refinery in Százhalombatta and later at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant), the prime minister outlined the government’s response to the unprecedented situation created by the Danube’s exceptionally low water level.

Paks could stop generating electricity next week

Magyar said the nuclear power station is currently operating at roughly 960 megawatts, less than half of its normal 2,000-megawatt capacity.

According to the government, the Danube stood at minus 124 centimetres on Friday, while the plant’s final operating reactor must be shut down if the river falls to minus 134 centimetres to comply with safety regulations.

Based on the latest forecasts, the final reactor may have to be taken offline on Tuesday or Wednesday, although Magyar warned that the country’s most difficult period is expected to begin as early as Monday.

The prime minister stressed repeatedly that the situation does not pose a nuclear safety risk. He said the shutdown procedure follows long-established safety protocols, while the reactors’ cooling systems will continue operating even after electricity generation stops.

Long shutdown possible as drought continues

Officials warned that the outage could last longer than initially expected. Current weather forecasts indicate little chance of significant rainfall across the Danube catchment area in the coming weeks, meaning water levels may remain below the threshold required to restart the reactors.

The government said experts are continuously monitoring the river, with emergency mobile pumps available if the water level falls further to ensure cooling water can still be supplied safely.

Government seeks to avoid blackouts

Magyar said the government’s top priority is preventing nationwide power outages. He urged Hungary’s largest industrial consumers to cut electricity usage, particularly between 5 PM and 10 PM, when demand is highest.

According to the prime minister, Thursday evening’s peak electricity demand was already 151 megawatts lower than forecast thanks to voluntary reductions, while MOL has committed to reducing its own electricity consumption by 65 megawatts.

Meanwhile, the Dunamenti Power Plant is expected to begin trial operations on Saturday after repairs, with around 400 megawatts of generating capacity scheduled to return by Sunday.

Photo: MTI

PM blames previous governments

Magyar argued that the current situation has been made worse by years of insufficient investment. He claimed the previous government failed to upgrade Paks after the Danube reached a record low in 2018, despite improvements being carried out at the Dunamenti Power Plant, where modifications to the water intake system have allowed operations to continue despite the current drought.

According to the prime minister, the temporary loss of Paks’ electricity production could cost the state budget around HUF 50 billion per month. He also criticised what he described as misinformation surrounding the crisis, urging political actors not to spread false claims or create unnecessary panic.

Climate change and energy policy under scrutiny

Magyar said the crisis illustrates how unprepared Hungary has been for the effects of climate change. He criticised previous governments for failing to accelerate investments in wind power, electricity storage and other renewable energy technologies, arguing that a more diversified energy system would have reduced the country’s dependence on both Russian technology and the Danube’s water level.

The government has already approved plans to allow the construction of new wind farms with a combined capacity roughly double that of the current Paks Nuclear Power Plant, he said.

If you missed it: Thousands lose water supply in Hungary as Paks output is cut and red warnings are issued

Emergency task force considers further measures

An emergency government defence task force was scheduled to meet on Friday evening to examine several contingency plans in case Paks is forced to shut down completely. Among the options under consideration is the possibility of restricting certain rail freight operations during peak demand periods to reduce pressure on the electricity grid.

The government is also assessing the availability of additional electricity imports from neighbouring countries to help maintain supply if domestic generation falls further.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

PM dismisses rumours over Danube and Ukraine

Magyar also rejected social media claims that neighbouring countries, including Austria, Germany and Slovakia, were deliberately withholding water from the Danube. According to the prime minister, neither the government nor Hungary’s water management authorities have found any evidence to support those allegations.

He likewise denied reports that Hungary is exporting electricity to Ukraine during the current energy crisis, saying the opposite is true in the present circumstances.

World.title: Hungary convenes emergency task force as heatwave puts water and energy systems under pressure
World.content:
The Hungarian government has convened an emergency meeting of its defence task force to address growing concerns over the country’s water and energy systems as an intense heatwave continues to grip Hungary. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said key decisions would be taken on Friday evening following consultations with ministers, infrastructure operators and regulators.

Emergency meeting to address water and energy challenges

Speaking at a press conference at MOL’s Danube Refinery in Százhalombatta, Magyar said the government would hold an emergency session of its defence task force on Friday evening to decide on the most urgent measures needed to respond to the developing situation.

According to the prime minister, the task force brings together members of the government, representatives of regulatory authorities, public agencies and the operators of Hungary’s critical infrastructure.

Before the meeting, Magyar said he would continue consultations with ministers, regulators and infrastructure leaders, including further discussions in Paks, where the government has been monitoring the impact of the Danube’s exceptionally low water level on the country’s energy supply. The government said it would announce the decisions taken after the meeting.

Government appeals for greater public cooperation

Magyar said Hungary’s water utility companies had prepared extensively for the heatwave and the increased demand for drinking water. However, he warned that many households were still ignoring official requests to reduce water consumption.

According to the prime minister, some residents have continued watering gardens and filling swimming pools despite repeated appeals to conserve water. He urged the public to avoid these activities over the coming days in order to help maintain a stable drinking water supply, describing uninterrupted water service as the government’s highest priority.

Companies asked to cut energy consumption further

The prime minister also renewed his appeal for voluntary energy-saving measures, particularly among large industrial consumers. He praised companies that have already announced reductions in electricity use, citing Samsung and the Budapest Municipality as examples. At the same time, he encouraged businesses to go even further.

“I ask companies to multiply those figures by two or three before sending us the email,” Magyar said, referring to the voluntary energy-saving commitments submitted to the government.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

“We have the situation under control”

Despite the mounting pressure caused by the prolonged heatwave, Magyar sought to reassure the public. “We have the situation under control, and it can remain under control,” he said. At the same time, he cautioned that the current period of extreme weather could last not only for several days but potentially for weeks. To minimise disruption and damage, he said, genuine cooperation between the government, businesses and the public would be essential.

World.title: Hungary population decline continues: country loses tens of thousands of people in 6 months
World.content:
Hungary’s population continued to decline during the first half of 2026, with births once again significantly outnumbered by deaths, according to the latest preliminary figures published by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH). While both the number of births and deaths fell compared with a year earlier, the country still recorded a natural population decrease of more than 28,000 people in the first six months of the year.

Fewer births and deaths in June

According to KSH, 5,790 children were born in June 2026, down 2.6% (157 births) from June last year. During the same month, 9,167 people died, representing a 3.1% decrease (291 fewer deaths) compared with June 2025.

As a result, Hungary’s natural population decline—the difference between births and deaths—stood at 3,377 people in June, slightly lower than the 3,511 recorded in the same month a year earlier. The number of marriages, however, increased. 4,942 couples married in June, up 8.9% year-on-year.

Population fell by more than 28,000 in first half of the year

According to KSH figures, between January and June 2026, a total of 34,312 children were born, 2.0% fewer than during the same period in 2025. Over the same six months, 62,330 people died, a 4.1% decrease compared with the previous year.

Despite the lower mortality rate, deaths continued to far exceed births, resulting in a natural population decline of 28,018 people. Although still substantial, this was 6.6% lower than the 29,994 recorded during the first half of 2025.

Fertility rate remains low

The figures also show that Hungary’s total fertility rate remained largely unchanged at 1.27 children per woman, slightly below last year’s 1.28.

During the first half of the year, there were 7.3 live births and 13.3 deaths per 1,000 inhabitants. The infant mortality rate stood at 4.1 deaths per 1,000 live births, marginally higher than a year earlier.

Marriages continue to rise

Marriage numbers were one of the few positive demographic indicators. A total of 21,177 couples married between January and June, an increase of 4.4% (895 marriages) compared with the same period in 2025.

On a rolling 12-month basis, from July 2025 to June 2026, 47,477 couples married, also marking a 4.0% increase over the previous 12 months.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Regional differences

The demographic trends varied across Hungary. Births declined in Budapest and three other regions but increased in four regions, with the strongest growth recorded in Northern Hungary. Budapest experienced the largest decline in births.

Deaths fell in every region except the Northern Great Plain, while the natural population decrease improved across all regions except Budapest. Marriage numbers increased in every region outside the capital, with Northern Hungary recording the strongest growth.

Although mortality continued to decline, the latest figures underline that Hungary’s long-term demographic challenges remain. The number of births is still well below the number of deaths, meaning the country’s population continues to shrink despite modest improvements in some indicators.

World.title: Man in custody after attacking train conductor on Budapest-Vienna service
World.content:
A Hungarian court has ordered the pre-trial detention of a man accused of violently attacking a train conductor on a Budapest–Vienna service, before allegedly threatening to kill the railway employee and resisting police officers at Komárom railway station.

The Tatabánya District Court ordered the suspect to remain in custody for one month on suspicion of committing violence against a person performing public duties, according to a statement issued by the court.

Alleged assault began during ticket inspection

Prosecutors say the incident took place on 28 July, when the man was travelling on a train from Budapest to Vienna.

According to the investigation, the conductor asked the passenger to present his ticket. The suspect was reportedly talking to himself before suddenly standing up and striking the conductor forcefully on the head and chest without any apparent provocation.

The conductor retreated into the train corridor, but investigators say the man followed him and repeatedly punched him across the body.

Emergency stop at Komárom

The train came to an emergency stop at Komárom railway station, where the suspect allegedly continued behaving aggressively.

According to the court, he threatened to kill the conductor even after the train had stopped.

When police officers arrived at the scene, the man reportedly shouted aggressively at them and refused repeated instructions to comply. Officers eventually restrained and handcuffed him using physical force.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Court cites flight risk and witness intimidation concerns

The court ruled that the legal conditions for pre-trial detention had been met because the offence carries a potential prison sentence. Judges also found there was a genuine risk that the suspect could flee or go into hiding. According to the court, there are indications that he intended to leave Hungary for an unknown destination before his arrest.

In addition, the court said there were reasonable grounds to believe that, if released, the suspect could intimidate or unlawfully influence witnesses who have yet to be questioned during the criminal proceedings. For these reasons, the court ordered his detention for one month. The decision is final.

World.title: Critical situation: PM Magyar and MOL CEO on Hungary’s fuel supplies, Russian oil, power station and tourist boats
World.content:
Hungary is preparing for a critical period in its energy system after Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is expected to be shut down from Monday due to the Danube’s exceptionally low water level. Speaking alongside MOL Chairman and CEO Zsolt Hernádi on Friday, the prime minister urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption as the country prepares for the unprecedented disruption.

Paks shutdown expected as Danube reaches critical levels

At an extraordinary press briefing held at MOL’s Danube Refinery in Százhalombatta, Magyar said the situation is likely to become critical from Monday.

The prime minister warned that another reduction in output at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is expected before the facility is completely taken offline. If this happens, it will mark the first full shutdown in the plant’s 44-year history caused by extremely low water levels in the Danube.

Magyar stressed that the decision is based solely on safety considerations and urged former Fidesz politicians to stop spreading what he described as misinformation suggesting the shutdown is unnecessary.

“Experts are not making these decisions lightly,” he said.

According to the prime minister, a full shutdown of Paks would result in an estimated HUF 50 billion loss per month for the Hungarian economy.

Government urges households and businesses to save electricity

Magyar highlighted that electricity demand peaks each day between 5 PM and 10 PM, calling on the public to reduce consumption during those hours whenever possible.

He also appealed to Hungary’s largest industrial energy users to cut their electricity use in preparation for Monday’s expected supply pressures.

The prime minister announced that MOL itself will reduce its energy consumption by 40%, adding that the government will provide the company with additional assistance to ensure the continued operation of critical fuel infrastructure.

Photo: MTI

Magyar: The ships and barges are stuck

“The ships are stuck—not just the tourist boats; even the barges can’t come in, and we can’t cool Paks,” Magyar listed some pressing problems. However, he said that in other European countries, it is possible to navigate the Danube. According to the prime minister, experts need to be brought in because the problem isn’t going to go away: it needs to be solved.

MOL: Hungary has sufficient fuel supplies

Speaking alongside the prime minister, Zsolt Hernádi, Chairman and CEO of MOL, sought to reassure the public that Hungary has adequate fuel reserves.

“There is enough fuel in Hungary,” he said, while acknowledging that the exceptionally low level of the Danube has created operational challenges for the country’s largest refinery.

Hernádi revealed that MOL had requested government assistance because of the critically low river level affecting logistics and refinery operations.

He also said the company is continuing preparations to reduce its dependence on Russian crude oil ahead of legislative changes due to take effect next year. However, he noted that uncertainty remains over the future capacity of the Adriatic Pipeline, making close cooperation with the government essential.

Asked about fuel prices, Hernádi declined to comment, saying any statement could influence the market. Magyar jokingly interrupted by saying, “I’ll talk about it,” prompting laughter as Hernádi replied that he could not stop the prime minister from doing so.

Danube power station returns to full capacity

Magyar also announced that the Dunamenti Power Plant is expected to return to full capacity on Saturday after the arrival of a replacement component, providing additional support to Hungary’s electricity system ahead of the expected Paks shutdown.

Government monitors water infrastructure

Beyond the energy sector, the prime minister warned that Hungary’s ageing water infrastructure is under increasing strain because of the prolonged heatwave and drought.

He said burst water mains are likely in the coming days, arguing that decades of underinvestment by previous governments have left the network vulnerable during periods of extreme demand.

Magyar added that the heads of Hungary’s critical infrastructure operators had been summoned for an emergency meeting later on Friday.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Hungary seeks regional cooperation over the Danube

The government is also looking beyond Hungary’s borders in response to the worsening drought.

Magyar said he had instructed Foreign Minister Anita Orbán to contact her counterparts in neighbouring countries to explore possible regional cooperation aimed at addressing the Danube’s rapidly falling water level.

While he did not outline specific measures, the move reflects growing concern over the impact of the prolonged drought on energy production, water supplies and transport across Central Europe.

World.title: Nscale to acquire Romanian co-founded AI startup Anyscale in reportedly USD 1.65 billion deal
World.content:
Cloud infrastructure provider Nscale will acquire AI software startup Anyscale, which has Romanian-born university professor Ion Stoica among its co-founders, in a transaction worth roughly USD 1.65 billion, according to a Bloomberg News source.

Ion Stoica is a co-founder of Anyscale, together with Robert Nishihara (chief executive officer) and Philipp Moritz (chief technology officer), who were his PhD students at RISELab within the University of California, Berkeley.

San Francisco-based Anyscale provides software for organizing and managing complex AI workloads so that they can run smoothly across multiple computers simultaneously. Nscale said it expects to attract more customers by offering Anyscale’s software.

Anyscale will continue to operate under its own brand and serve its existing customers, the companies said. Anyscale’s entire team of approximately 200 people across the United States, Europe and India will join Nscale as part of the acquisition.

The transaction is expected to be completed in the second half of this year, the companies said.

Anyscale recorded revenue growth of 70% compared with the previous quarter in the company’s most recent quarter, according to a blog post by its co-founders.

Originally from Romania, Stoica left for the United States in the late 1990s to pursue his PhD at Carnegie Mellon University. Since 2000, he has been teaching at UC Berkeley, where he leads a laboratory funded largely by technology companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google, and IBM, with an annual budget of more than USD 6 million.

Stoica became a billionaire by launching four startups that originated from his research laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. The most valuable of them, Databricks and Anyscale, started as open-source projects within the university. The first was valued at USD 134 billion earlier this year.

Before Databricks, Stoica also co-founded video streaming startup Conviva.

World.title: UNICEF, Romanian Labor Ministry launch e-Learning HUB for professionals in social assistance
World.content:
Romania’s Labor Ministry and UNICEF announced the launch of e-Learning HUB, a national platform dedicated to the continuous professional training of personnel in the field of social services and sectors that contribute to social inclusion.

The HUB provides coordinated access to training opportunities, educational resources and professional development programs. The platform brings together continuous professional training opportunities for specialists in the social field, covering essential topics such as the protection of vulnerable persons, human rights, digital skills and quality standards in social services.

The HUB is designed to become the digital foundation of the future National Center for Continuous Training in Social Assistance, which is scheduled to become operational in 2028. The platform will contribute to increasing the skills of professionals in social assistance and related fields, personnel of central and local public authorities with responsibilities in the social field, decision-makers, accredited professional training providers, professional organizations, and non-governmental organizations active in the field of social assistance and the protection of human rights.

“Through e-Learning HUB, specialists across the country will be able to identify relevant courses more easily, develop their skills and have access to modern resources adapted to the real needs of the system,” said Silvia Dinică, State Secretary within the Labor Ministry.

“Professionals in social services are facing increasingly complex challenges, from poverty and social exclusion to the effects of recent crises on children and families. The e-Learning HUB platform offers a single access point to quality learning opportunities and represents an important step toward strengthening the workforce in the social field,” said Anna Riatti, UNICEF Representative in Romania.

The e-Learning HUB will facilitate access to accredited training programs, promote collaboration between institutions and training providers, and support the development of the skills needed to provide integrated and quality services.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Bucharest Community Foundation and City Hall begin transforming Herăstrău Park through public-private collaboration
World.content:
Bucharest City Hall and the Bucharest Community Foundation announced on Friday, July 31, that they have begun transforming the city’s major northern park, Herăstrău, according to the priorities expressed by nearly 10,000 participants in the public consultation.

The process benefits from private funding worth EUR 900,000 already mobilized by the Bucharest Community Foundation. The first EUR 90,000 will be invested in the studies and expertise required for the regeneration of the park’s green spaces, with the remainder to be directed as the stages are established together with the public administration.

The funds will cover the tree inventory through a TreePlotter-type digital application, the creation of a public inventory, specialized studies, technical and dendrological expertise, assessment of tree health and risk, preparation of the tree management plan, as well as the documentation needed to establish design requirements for future interventions.

The digital tree inventory will be public and accessible both to the administration and citizens and will form the basis of a Green Register dedicated to Old Herăstrău Park. For each tree, GIS location, dendrometric characteristics, health status, and management recommendations will be recorded. Data can be permanently updated by the public administration, and the tool can be gradually expanded to the entire Herăstrău Park, providing a permanent instrument for monitoring and adaptive and sustainable management of tree heritage.

The two partners began working together through a new collaboration model that brings together public administration, the community, specialists and private funders. The new working mechanism allows preparatory stages to begin quickly, independently of the public budget calendar, while maintaining decision-making, control and ownership of the documentation within the public administration.

The Bucharest Community Foundation will finance and contract specialists for the regeneration of green spaces based on specifications agreed with the authorities and experts involved, while the results will be handed over to the Bucharest City Hall and will serve as the basis for future design and construction works.

Meanwhile, the two partners will prepare the administrative framework for major interventions and mobilize the private sector and civil society to attract the financial resources necessary for the subsequent stages of the regeneration process. Private resources will accelerate project preparation without transferring decision-making rights over the park to funders. Control, validation and ownership of documentation will remain the responsibility of the public administration, while intervention solutions and priorities will be defined in collaboration with specialists, funders and community members, in accordance with the principles of the New European Bauhaus.

Going forward, the Bucharest Community Foundation aims to attract funds of up to EUR 10 million from the private sector and civil society for the subsequent intervention plan.

“If we waited for the completion of administrative procedures for landscape design, as well as for securing the lakeside area, we would not have enough speed. That is why I cannot sufficiently emphasize the role of the Bucharest Community Foundation. My role was to be open to collaboration and, together, to create this mechanism through which we can get on track, set things in motion, and accelerate interventions,” said Bucharest mayor Ciprian Ciucu.

Public consultation

The planned works follow a public consultation carried out between May and June 2026, in which nearly half of respondents said that they were dissatisfied with the current state of the park.

Participants’ expectations were very concrete. Modernization of general infrastructure was considered a priority by 83.2% of respondents, while 74.3% indicated the restoration of the natural environment as one of the main intervention directions. Permanent public toilets, more numerous and cleaner, represented the most requested specific measure resulting from the consultation, indicated by 85.5% of respondents. Better lighting at night was desired by 81.4% of respondents, followed by the rehabilitation of paths and paving (77.9%), ensuring functional drinking fountains (68.9%) and improving urban furniture (61.6%).

Restoring the natural environment was equally important. Among the respondents, 78.6% requested more trees and denser vegetation for shade, cooling and air filtration, while 71.2% wanted improved lake water quality, and 56.9% wanted better access to the waterfront. Nearly half of participants mentioned degraded paths and sidewalks among the main complaints, while responses indicate a clear preference for preserving the park’s natural character and avoiding excessive interventions.

World.title: Over 6 in 10 Romanians cannot afford a one-week annual vacation
World.content:
Romania ranks first in the European Union in terms of the share of people who cannot afford a one-week annual vacation away from home, according to data published by Eurostat on Thursday, July 30.

According to the European Statistical Office, 61.4% of Romanians aged 16 or older said they could not afford a one-week vacation away from home in 2025. Romania is followed by Greece, where 46.6% of residents were in the same situation, and by Bulgaria and Hungary, both with 39.1%.

The difference from the European Union average is significant. Across the 27 member states, 27.5% of people aged over 16 said they could not afford a one-week holiday away from home.

Compared with 2024, the share of people who cannot afford a vacation increased by 0.5% across the European Union. However, the long-term trend remains positive. Compared with 2015, the indicator has fallen by 7.7%, so over the last decade more and more Europeans have gained the financial ability to go on holiday for at least one week a year.

At the other end of the ranking are the states where an annual vacation is accessible to the vast majority of the population. The lowest share of people unable to afford a one-week holiday was recorded in Luxembourg, where only 10.6% of residents said they could not cover such an expense. It is followed by Sweden, with 12.4%, and the Netherlands, with 12.8%, values almost five times lower than those reported in Romania.

The ability to spend at least one week a year on vacation away from home is one of the indicators used by Eurostat to assess living conditions and the level of material deprivation in the member states. The data highlight the persistent differences between European economies in terms of purchasing power and households’ ability to cover expenses considered normal for a decent standard of living.

World.title: Romania launches national campaign to promote its 13 national parks
World.content:
The Ministry of Environment and the Conservation Carpathia Foundation have launched a nationwide campaign to promote Romania’s 13 national parks and raise public awareness about their environmental and economic value. The campaign, titled Parks for Generations (Parcurile Generațiilor), was launched during the Făgăraș Fest festival and will run on television, radio, and digital platforms.

The initiative seeks to explain the difference between national parks and other natural or urban parks, encouraging Romanians to visit the protected areas while highlighting their role in biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, and local development.

Romania's 13 national parks protect around 317,500 hectares of land, including forests, alpine meadows, gorges, and caves that provide habitats for numerous rare plant and animal species. According to Conservation Carpathia, the parks also help regulate water cycles, reduce the risks of droughts and floods, and support local economies through tourism-related activities.

The national parks are Buila-Vânturarița, Călimani, Ceahlău, Bicaz Gorges-Hășmaș, Nera Gorges-Beușnița, Cozia, Jiu Gorge, Domogled-Cerna Valley, Măcin Mountains, Rodna Mountains, Piatra Craiului, Retezat, and Semenic-Caraș Gorges.

The campaign follows research showing that public understanding of national parks remains limited. A 2024 study by Unlock Market Research found that while 67% of Romanians said they had visited a national park, many confused them with nature reserves, natural parks, or other protected areas. Another finding showed that 82% of respondents could not define what distinguishes a national park from other forms of nature protection.

“National parks are among the most remarkable places Romania has. They protect nature, but they also create opportunities for local communities and future generations," said Barbara and Christoph Promberger, executive directors of the Conservation Carpathia Foundation.

“We want more Romanians to discover them, understand their value and be proud that Romania has such a rich natural heritage. People protect what they know and appreciate, and that is the first step we want to take together," they added.

In her turn, interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said the campaign aims to address the public's limited knowledge of Romania’s protected areas.

“Romania has national parks with almost a century of history. […] Yet recent data show that too few Romanians know what a national park really is and the role it plays for nature, climate, water, local communities, and the economy," the minister said.

“The Parks for Generations campaign does exactly this: it brings national parks closer to the public and explains, in accessible language, why these places are so important for Romania," she added.

The campaign includes a dedicated online platform featuring information about all 13 national parks, visitor recommendations, and links to each park's official website. It was developed by creative agency Pastel for the Conservation Carpathia Foundation and the Ministry of Environment, with support from the Romanian Rangers Association.

The Conservation Carpathia Foundation is one of Europe's largest private nature conservation initiatives, working to restore ecosystems in Romania's Southern Carpathian Mountains. Since its establishment in 2009, the foundation has acquired more than 28,000 hectares of forests and alpine meadows for conservation, planted over 4.5 million trees on nearly 2,000 hectares of degraded land, and created a 78,000-hectare no-hunting zone.

Its long-term goal is to support the creation of the Făgăraș Mountains National Park, while promoting biodiversity conservation alongside sustainable economic development for local communities.

World.title: Canada’s Alimentation Couche-Tard to acquire controlling stake in Polish Żabka Group, owner of Froo stores in Romania
World.content:
Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. (TSX: ATD) announced that it plans to acquire a controlling stake in Poland's largest convenience retailer Żabka Group (WSE: ZAB) in a deal valued at USD 8.6 billion.

Couche-Tard will initiate a voluntary tender offer through its wholly owned subsidiary, Circle K Polska sp. z.o.o. for PLN 32.00 (equivalent of USD 8.48) per share, representing a total equity value of approximately PLN 32.62 billion (equivalent of USD 8.6 billion).

The transaction represents the largest acquisition in Couche-Tard’s history, the company said.

The deal is supported by Żabka's key executive managers and shareholders owning, in aggregate, approximately 57% of Żabka's issued and outstanding shares, including CVC Capital Partners and Partners Group.

For Couche-Tard, the acquisition will add an immediate, scaled platform in Central and Eastern Europe, it said.

The Canadian company plans to preserve Żabka's management structure, brand, entrepreneurial franchise model and local expertise.

Couche-Tard expects to fund the transaction through fully committed debt facilities underwritten by J.P. Morgan as Lead Arranger, with National Bank of Canada Capital Markets and The Bank of Nova Scotia acting as Joint Bookrunners.

The transaction is subject to receipt of regulatory approvals, including merger control approval by the European Commission or Polish Prezes Urzędu Konkurencji i Konsumentów (UOKiK), foreign direct investment approval by Romanian Comisia pentru examinarea investiţiilor străine directe, and approval under the European Union's Foreign Subsidies Regulation by the European Commission.

If Couche-Tard reaches at least 95% of the total voting rights in Żabka, it intends to initiate a compulsory acquisition (squeeze-out) of the remaining shares and take the necessary steps to procure the delisting of Żabka's shares from the Warsaw Stock Exchange.

Founded in 1998 and listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange since October 2024, Żabka Group operates more than 13,000 convenience stores across Poland and Romania and services approximately 4.3 million average daily transactions. Its network is built around compact, modular neighborhood stores averaging approximately 65 sqm, located across urban, suburban and rural communities to serve immediate consumption and everyday convenience needs.

Zabka is present in Romania with a network of stores opened under the brand Froo, which it launched locally in 2024.

The company opened 778 new stores across Poland and Romania in the first half of 2026, including 706 in Poland and 72 in Romania, bringing the total to 13,063 stores at end-June 2026, up 10.8% YoY. In Q2, the group opened 343 new stores, including 303 in Poland and 40 in Romania.
