Cooler operating conditions over water also reduce soiling losses and can improve panel efficiency.

The Cabinet note says the scheme will also encourage domestic manufacturing of specialised components while generating an estimated 16,000-17,000 jobs.

Cost and engineering

The technology, however, comes at a premium. Government estimates place floating solar system costs at ₹4.9-5.2 crore per MW, about 25% higher than comparable ground-mounted projects due to the additional expenditure on floating platforms, anchoring and mooring systems.

The mandatory battery storage further increases project costs. Developers have also reported engineering challenges at existing projects, including wear on floating structures and cable failures. The Centre nevertheless expects the higher upfront costs to be offset by the strategic value of creating a geographically diversified solar fleet with integrated storage reducing dependence on land-intensive projects while making renewable electricity more dispatchable.

World.title: The Hindu brings the historic 1947 Independence Day edition back to life
World.content:
When India awoke to freedom on the morning of August 15, 1947, The Hindu was there to chronicle the birth of a newly independent nation. Now, as the country prepares to celebrate its 80th Independence Day, the publication is offering readers a rare opportunity to step back into that exact moment in time.

To honour this defining milestone, The Hindu has reproduced its landmark August 15, 1947, edition in its entirety. The original 32-page edition has been meticulously reproduced exactly as it appeared nearly eight decades ago.

Within its pages, readers will find rare photographs documenting the hard-fought freedom struggle and the country’s first proud steps forward. It features deeply personal Independence Day greetings from monumental figures including Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

Alongside these historic messages are vivid, on-the-ground reports of the very first flag-hoisting ceremonies that swept the nation. Even the vintage s offer a fascinating, nostalgic glimpse into India’s social and commercial landscape of the era.

Starting August 1, 2026, limited copies of this collector’s edition will be available exclusively on Zepto across major Indian cities. It is a unique chance to own and hold history in your hands.

World.title: Kochi metro records operational profit, lowers net loss
World.content:
Kochi Metro Rail Limited (KMRL) claimed to have registered an operational profit of ₹52.64 crore in 2025-26. The year also saw its net loss fall from ₹430.50 crore in 2024–25 to ₹352.49 crore, said a KMRL release.

The operational profit will go up when the metro’s second phase connecting the city with Smart City and Infopark in Kakkanad is commissioned, hoped KMRL managing director Loknath Behera.

The metro also saw average daily ridership crossing the one-lakh mark during the year, reaching 1.01 lakh passengers.

Of the total operational revenue of ₹224.65 crore, ₹76.33 crore (nearly 34%) came from non-fare sources.

World.title: Supreme Court asks Centre to facilitate DNA testing of Indians killed in Russia-Ukraine war
World.content:
The Supreme Court on Friday (July 31, 2026) directed the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) to appoint a nodal officer to facilitate DNA testing of the mortal remains of Indian nationals killed on the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, ensuring families can claim them for last rites.

A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant asked the Ministry to forward the details of the nodal officer to the family members of the deceased once the appointment is made.

The court was hearing a petition filed by families alleging their kin were victims of illegal overseas recruitment, trafficking, and exploitation. According to the petitioners, the youths were lured by recruiters with promises of high-paying jobs, only to have their passports seized and be pushed into the war zone.

The petitioners sought the whereabouts of Indian nationals believed to be dead or missing, urging the court to intervene for the repatriation of bodies and the payment of monetary compensation by Russian authorities.

Compensation claims

The court on Friday (July 31) ruled that complete records for filing compensation claims with Russian authorities must be provided to the families, who can submit their claims through the Ministry. The Bench added that families should receive legal aid for these filings, along with DNA verification certificates and translated versions of any Russian documents.

The court clarified that compensation claims should not become a ground for delaying the handing over of mortal remains or the performance of funeral rituals.

Diplomatic efforts

The Union government informed the court that nearly 220 Indians had joined the Russian Armed Forces during the conflict, with 139 released from contractual agreements.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre, stated that the government successfully negotiated with Russian authorities for the discharge of Indian nationals. Out of the 51 Indians died in the battleground, the remains of 29 individuals have been brought back to India, she added.

The petitioners also highlighted the necessity of identifying and prosecuting illegal overseas recruitment rackets that exploit vulnerable citizens with false promises of foreign employment.

World.title: Kin of injured Delhi police personnel want their views to be discussed in Parliament
World.content:
Family members of four Delhi Police personnel who were injured during the crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led march to Parliament on July 20, demanding the resignation of then Education Minister Dhrmendra Pradhan, on Friday (July 31, 2026) called for a discussion in Parliament on the injuries suffered by the policemen on duty. They said the public discourse so far has been “one-sided”.

Addressing a press conference at the Constitution Club, the family members—the wives of an ACP and an ASI, and the children of two injured police officers—took turns to recount what had transpired that day and said that “their side of the story” of the June 20 violence needed to be heard.

Slideshow presented

The families presented photographs of injured and bleeding police personnel through a slideshow, that claimed that more than 250 police personnel were injured in the violence, while over 110 barricades, 300 body protectors, 350 helmets, 20 loudhailers, 10 hand-held metal detectors and one X-ray baggage scanner were damaged, with more than 25 government vehicles and private property vandalised.

They alleged that several anti-social elements had joined the students who attacked the policemen.

The wife of an ASI who sustained injuries during the violence said, “Students should be released after their records are verified, but the miscreants who attempted to disrupt the students’ protest, tarnish its image and undermine the dignity of Parliament should be held accountable for their actions and should not be spared.”

A Delhi University student whose father, a sub-inspector, was injured in the clashes, said he had served for 15 years as a Marine Commando in the Indian Navy before joining the police. She said that her father returned home with his uniform soaked in blood, but when she opened social media, he had already been declared a criminal.

Another family member of an injured ACP said, “Whenever I go online, I see videos portraying only the police as criminals. There is no discussion, even in Parliament, about the police personnel who were injured. We only want our side to be heard.”

Several questions have been raised over the alleged use of excessive force against protesters during the July 20 march. Videos circulating on social media name and identify some of the men in uniform using excessive force, while some clips also show police personnel in plain clothes wielding batons.

On July 28, the Supreme Court observed that it would consider constituting a high-powered investigating team to conduct a “thorough, fair and independent” inquiry into allegations of police excesses during the recent student protests in Delhi.

World.title: Triumph of justice vs Hussain a BJP man: parties trade barbs after Tahir Hussain verdict
World.content:
A war of words broke out between the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) on Friday (July 31, 2026) following the sentencing of former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain and four others to life imprisonment for the murder of Intelligence Bureau officer Ankit Sharma during the 2020 north-east Delhi riots.

While the BJP hailed the court order for “establishing how AAP-backed miscreants spread riots in north-east Delhi”, the Opposition party hit back, claiming that Hussain was “indirectly working for the BJP”.

Welcoming the order, Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said people in Delhi are now demanding answers from AAP.

“Tahir Hussain was arrested on charges of murder, yet even after that, [AAP chief Arvind] Kejriwal and [AAP leader] Manish Sisodia stood in his support! They kept trying relentlessly to save him! Why? Will Mr. Kejriwal tell the people of Delhi? Was it under their patronage that people like Tahir Hussain conspired to incite riots? Today, justice has triumphed. This verdict further strengthens the faith of every citizen of the country in the law and the judiciary,” Ms. Gupta posted on X.

Delhi BJP president Harsh Malhotra said, “Kejriwal should be ashamed for not only sheltering such criminals within the party but also for repeatedly using his influence to protect them. The true character of the Aam Aadmi Party is now well understood not only by the people of Delhi but also by the people of Punjab.”

Delhi Law Minister Kapil Mishra said the sentencing was “the beginning of justice”.

‘Hussain a BJP man’

Addressing a press conference, AAP’s State unit chief Saurabh Bharadwaj said his party had expelled Hussain as soon as an FIR was registered against him in the Ankit Sharma murder case. Mr. Bharadwaj said Hussain had contested the Mustafabad Assembly election last year on an All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen ticket as part of a “well-planned strategy by the BJP” against AAP.

“There are dozens of instances where the BJP has embraced individuals involved in the most heinous crimes. In reality, Tahir Hussain was a BJP man. If anyone gained political advantage from the Delhi riots, it was the BJP,” said the former Health Minister.

He accused Mr. Mishra, who was earlier with AAP, of backing Hussain and propping him up as a politician. “Kapil Mishra’s own election office and MLA office were located in Tahir Hussain’s house, where weapons or stones allegedly used in the riots were found stored. It was Kapil Mishra who inducted Tahir Hussain into the party [AAP],” said the senior AAP leader.

World.title: Govt cuts petrol price by 12 paisas, diesel by 66 paisas for the next three days
World.content:
The government on Friday reduced the prices of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by 12 paisas and 66 paisas per litre, respectively.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs336.03 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs392.38 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs110 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs96 per litre on diesel.

The Petroleum Division’s notification said that the new prices would be applicable from August 1 to August 3.

Meanwhile, in a bigger price shock, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) notified a record 32pc increase in the price of regasified liquefied natural gas (RLNG) for August, taking it to $25.83 per mmBtu for SNGPL and $25.09 per mmBtu for SSGCL.

This will translate into a retail price of Rs7,204 per mmBtu. The price is based on five imported cargoes from the spot market, as no shipment could be secured from Qatar because of the US-Iran war. This is the single biggest jump in RLNG rates in its decade-long history.

This comes on top of an about 15pc increase in the RLNG price fixed last month at $19.52 per mmBtu (Rs5,446 per mmBtu) for SNGPL and $18.63 per mmBtu for SSGCL.

Compared with $10.45 (Rs2,916) per mmBtu in February this year, the RLNG price hike works out to around 148pc for August.

This mainly results in a substantial increase in fuel costs for power generation. This can be seen from the fact that the fuel cost for RLNG-based power generation in May worked out to Rs31 per unit, compared with Rs13.72 per unit in April.

The diesel price has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

The daily pricing decision was rejected by the All Pakistan Dealers Association, which said it would consider a protest plan this week.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Search operation for climbers missing after Broad Peak avalanche suspended due to bad weather
World.content:
GILGIT: The search and rescue operation for foreign climbers missing after an avalanche at Broad Peak was suspended late Friday due to adverse weather conditions in the region.

Three bodies of missing climbers — one each from the United States, Nepal and Oman — were airlifted from Broad Peak to Skardu by Pakistan Army helicopters. Drone footage also indicated the presence of more climbers during the search operation.

Earlier reports had said that four bodies were recovered; however, the toll was later revised down to three. Seven climbers remain missing.

According to a press release issued by the Commissioner Baltistan Division, the search and rescue operation was launched following a formal request from tour operators.

A three-member civil rescue team, led by renowned mountaineer Sarbaz Khan, was airlifted to Broad Peak Base Camp by Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters.

The team recovered the bodies of three climbers, identified as Oman’s Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy, Nepal’s Pur Bahadur Gurung and Mallory Geis from the United States. The bodies were later shifted to CMH Skardu by Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters.

The press release said the rescue operation had been temporarily suspended due to poor weather conditions and would resume on Saturday once conditions improved. Other Sherpas involved in mountaineering expeditions at the peak would also assist in the operation.

The rescue team said signs indicating the presence of more climbers had also been spotted through drone footage.

Despite the challenging terrain and harsh weather conditions at such high altitudes, the search operation was continuing with the cooperation of the Pakistan Army, local expert mountaineers and rescue teams.

The Gilgit-Baltistan government expressed condolences to the families of the deceased climbers and assured them that all possible assistance would be provided in the rescue operation and the repatriation of the bodies to their respective countries.

Experts said the chances of survival for the missing climbers were diminishing with each passing hour.

Earlier, the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) said that the 10-member team included six Nepalese climbers, a Pakistani, an Omani, an American and a climber from China. The climbers from Nepal were identified as renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja, Pur Bahadur Gurung, Kili Pemba Sherpa, Nima Sherpa, Nawang Thindu Sherpa and Gyalu Sherpa.

It identified the remaining climbers as Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman, Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi, Wang Zhong from China and Mallory Geis from the United States.

Rescue operation

In a statement issued earlier in the day, ACP Senior Vice President Karrar Haidri said two Pakistan Army Aviation rescue helicopters, carrying rescue personnel and additional specialised equipment, had been dispatched to support the ongoing search and rescue operation.

The statement said the ACP president, along with the club’s senior leadership, remained in constant contact with the highest government authorities and relevant agencies to facilitate the rescue operation.

“Every possible effort is being made to ensure that helicopter support and all available rescue resources are mobilised at the earliest opportunity, subject to weather and operational conditions,” it added.

The club said it was closely monitoring the situation and coordinating with all relevant stakeholders while expressing solidarity with the climbers’ families and the international mountaineering community.

ACP’s General Secretary Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that several expedition teams had jointly begun their summit push before the incident.

He said GPS locations received from some of the missing climbers indicated that the avalanche had swept the group about 1,000 metres downhill, leaving them trapped.

Shigri said there were also fears that some local high-altitude porters might have been affected by the avalanche.

“We pray for the safety of all the climbers. It is a big incident,” he said.

Meanwhile, Gilgit-Baltistan Chief Minister Amjad Hussain Advocate directed all relevant departments to remain on high alert and expedite the search and rescue operation in coordination with the Pakistan Army, according to an official statement.

He instructed the district administration and concerned authorities to utilise all available resources to ensure the climbers’ safety.

Gilgit-Baltistan Minister for Tourism, Sports and Culture Naiknam Karim also expressed sorrow over the incident and said the provincial government was making every possible effort to locate and safely rescue the missing climbers.

In a statement, he said “all relevant departments are in constant coordination and that every available resource was being utilised to support the ongoing search and rescue operation”.

Expressing hope that the missing climbers would be found safe, the minister directed the concerned authorities to further expedite the rescue operation and ensure that all necessary logistical and operational support was provided to the teams working in the field.

Purja, 43, who served with Britain’s Brigade of Gurkhas before joining the elite Special Boat Service (SBS), has broken multiple climbing records since becoming a full-time mountaineer and tour guide.

He climbed all 14 “eight-thousanders” (peaks above 8,000 metres, or 26,000 feet) in six months and six days between April and October 2019 — then a record. In 2021, Purja completed the first winter ascent of K2 along with a team of nine other Nepalese climbers.

Separately, in a post on X, the UK Embassy in Pakistan expressed concern at the incident. Seemingly referencing Purja, it also took note of a British-Nepali national missing in the expedition.

“We are concerned by reports that several climbers have gone missing during a Broad Peak expedition, including a British-Nepali national,” the embassy said, adding that it remained in contact with Pakistani authorities.

Sakhi, who hails from Hunza, had successfully summited Kanchenjunga (8,58­6m), the world’s 3rd highest mountain, in Nepal earlier in May. He had previously scaled K2, Nanga Parbat, Gasherbrum I and Gasherbrum II without supplemental oxygen, establishing himself among the country’s strongest high-altitude climbers.

Additional input from AFP

World.title: Good governance 'quintessential' for security and stability of Pakistan: DG ISPR
World.content:
Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry on Friday termed good governance “quintessential” for Pakistan’s security and stability.

He made the remarks while addressing a press conference on the country’s overall security situation, particularly the situation in Balochistan.

The DG ISPR, during his presser, commented on Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s remarks about the need for new administrative units in Pakistan: “We have been saying this earlier also as a primary stakeholder in security that good governance is essential for the security and stability of Pakistan.”

Without this, he stressed that none of Pakistan’s issues could be resolved.

The military spokesperson said the National Action Plan (NAP), with its 14-point agenda and the consensus of all political parties, required good governance for its implementation, adding, “Good governance is quintessential for Pakistan.”

“Now, how to achieve good governance? The politicians and political parties have to decide. If you ask us, yes, there has to be a serious discussion on it.”

“Now our population is 240-250 million people, and we still have four provinces. We have to see whether this is serving the purpose of good governance. That debate has to be sensibly held by politicians, by those in power, even those who have previously been in power, and those who are responsible to the people of Pakistan,” the DG ISPR said, adding that it had to be done according to the will of the people of Pakistan.

“The will of the people of Pakistan is superior. If good governance requires an administrative reset, then it has to be done through constitutional methods, legal procedures and political representatives.”

10 terrorists killed per day in 2026

At the outset of the briefing, the military spokesperson said 40,348 intelligence-based operations had been conducted this year so far, adding that the figure included operations carried out by all security forces, including police, civil armed forces, intelligence agencies and the armed forces.

Of these operations, the majority were carried out in Balochistan, with the number exceeding 31,000, he said.

The DG ISPR added that a total of 3,145 terrorism incidents had taken place in the country in 2026, of which 1,971 were reported from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 1,148 from Balochistan and 26 from other parts of the country.

During this period, he continued, 2,084 confirmed terrorists were killed. “This comes to an average of 10 terrorists being killed every day, which is the highest ratio ever,” he added.

Meanwhile, security forces were undertaking nearly 200 intelligence-based operations (IBOs) a day. “So these IBOs are going on every hour.”

The DG ISPR further stated that “819 Pakistanis have been martyred” in incidents of terrorism during the ongoing year, which amounted to four a day. This comprised 303 army personnel, 194 law enforcers, including police and civil armed forces personnel, and 322 civilians.

He added that 28 suicide bombing incidents had taken place this year, “the majority of which were carried out by Afghan nationals […] and people associated with their security forces”.

Comparing the figures for terrorists killed last year and in 2026, he said 2,597 were killed in 2025 and 2,084 this year so far.

Pointing out that five months were left before 2026 would end, he said, “The way the kinetic prong of the counter-terrorism is maturing, responding and delivering, that is before you.”

He further elaborated that the number of martyrs in comparison to slain terrorists was higher, but the tide started turning in 2024. And in 2025, “for each martyr we were taking out minimum two [terrorists], and this year, we are taking out minimum 2.5 [terrorists].”

Here, he added, a valid question to ask would be why terrorism incidents were rising. “Because once returns from other elements of their strategy begin diminishing, they focus more here. And you saw when their direct strategy during Marka-i-Haq failed, they started investing a lot more here,” he explained.

The DG ISPR added that this also had to do with the “agenda of the terrorist-supporting Taliban regime” and the clarity demonstrated by the state of Pakistan.

“These terrorists and their sponsors have come to understand that there is no space for appeasement or any talks with them […] They know that the state is telling them very clearly that either you submit to the state’s will in accordance with the law and the Constitution, or we are here and fighting,” he said.

Moreover, he added, this also had to do with the proactive nature of the operations. “These [terrorism] incidents also rise because when we get proactive […] there will be more engagements.”

Speaking of the “perception that the situation in Balochistan has worsened”, he said the matter would be examined through three questions.

The first question was what the issue was, the second was what was happening and the third was what was being done, he said.

Coming to the first question, he said the issue was not specific to Balochistan alone but related to the overall security environment in Pakistan.

The issue, he said, was “Hard state, question mark”.

“Are we a hard state? Unfortunately, not,” the military’s spokesperson added. Explaining the reason behind his answer, he said a hard state was one where the Constitution and the law applied equally to everyone. “That is what a hard state is. It does not mean a military-run state; it does not mean an armed forces-dominated state,” he added.

The DG ISPR said a state where all matters were decided in accordance with the Constitution and the law, where everyone was equal, was a hard state. In such a state, there would be security and stability, and there would be no grievances.

Then there was also the matter of obligations versus rights, he said, adding that it pertained to being aware of one’s responsibilities before speaking about one’s rights.

“We are all taking up grievances — at some places slogans are also being raised in connection with those grievances and even arms are being taken up in some instances — and all those grievances [pertain to demands for rights],” he said.

Saying that the demands for rights and the grievances may be genuine, he added that obligations needed to be fulfilled first.

“Let me try to explain the context constitutionally,” he said, quoting Article 5 of the Constitution.

The provision came before Article 8, which elaborated on fundamental rights, he said, adding that Article 5 stated: “Loyalty to the state and obedience to the Constitution and law. It says loyalty to the state is the basic duty of every citizen. Full stop. Absolutely clear.”

“The second part of the provision states that obedience to the Constitution and law is the inviolable obligation of every citizen wherever he may be.”

So the Constitution was “clear that we have some fundamental duties, including the need to be loyal to the state”.

“If we are loyal to the state and we are obedient to the Constitution and the law, then you can talk about your rights,” he said. Citing a statement by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at the National Workshop in Balochistan recently, he said when the rights movement is talked about, why not an “obligations movement”.

“There has to be a movement for the obligation of every citizen,” he asserted.

Further speaking of the obligations, he said, “Is this not an obligation for every citizen that our first and final identity should be Pakistani? … We are citizens of this state, so our first identity and our last identity and the foremost identity is being a Pakistani.

“It is our obligation to acknowledge the fundamental position, the central position of the state of Pakistan because if there is the state, there is politics, there is life […] These are our fundamental obligations.

“Are we working towards that? Let’s think about it.”

Focusing on Balochistan, he said the fundamental issues in the province were elitism, sardarism and the desire to maintain the status quo.

“This is that part of society which believes it has no obligations and only thinks of its rights. The elites and the sardars are a part of it. And I am not talking about all of them, but those who believe that this status quo must be maintained,” the DG ISPR said.

He added that this status quo predated 1947, under which a poor man’s child could not get an education or progress in life.

Those who did not want the status quo to change were the “prime movers of terrorism because they are afraid that the times are changing”.

Then there was the issue of the desire for appeasement, the DG ISPR said.

“They carry out terrorism, they talk about terrorism and say that Balochistan is getting out of hand. Then they expect that we talk to them and appease them […] No, we will not. We will talk with the actual stakeholders, who are the people of Balochistan,” he added.

“You are not the stakeholder. You are only a stakeholder in your own and your family’s fortunes.”

The military’s spokesperson went on to say that the problem with such elements was that they were not being appeased. “They have this habit of thinking that the Levies force is their private force, their sardari force.”

“So once you start turning Balochistan’s Levies into a police force, they have a problem.”

He further said that these elements were involved in smuggling in the name of business. “And if you stop this, there is terrorism. They promote terrorism and say Balochistan is getting out of hand.”

Moving on, the DG ISPR said a third issue was “external power play”.

The “elitists and sardarists have a common agenda”, he said, adding that “external powers” realised that Balochistan was blessed not only with “a very vibrant and very progressive human resource” but also with natural resources.

“It has a blue economy, agriculture. They know the potential of Balochistan. They realise that when Balochistan rises, the whole of Pakistan rises and the region rises. And they have a problem, so they get physically involved through these terrorists […] and they find ready partners in these elitists and sardarists,” he said.

Moreover, there was the issue of “contiguous support bases”, especially from Afghanistan.

He said the business of the Afghan Taliban regime was terrorism and that, through terrorism, it sustained its economy, state and even diplomacy.

“Even their diplomacy is centred on terrorism. What is common between India and Afghanistan, except their DNA? The only thing common is terrorism,” he added.

“What is common between Fitna-al-Hindustan and Fitna-al-Khawarij? Nothing. One is secular and nationalist, and the other is hardcore religious extremist. But because they are carrying out coordinated operations now…” he said.

The government labelled the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan as Fitna-al-Khawarij and designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan.

He further stated that propaganda was another issue, which, he said, had three strands: a sense of deprivation, lack of representation and missing persons.

Sharing data on facilities in various areas of Balochistan, he said the province’s per capita budget was more than Rs75,000, which was higher than that of any other province.

“Then on what basis is this narrative of a sense of deprivation in Balochistan spun? It is spun on actions to prevent development. That is why they kill labourers and attack roads, hospitals and bridges. Are these military targets?” the DG ISPR questioned.

Coming to the issue of lack of representation, he said same people and their families were in the assemblies since 1973. “Most of them are the same khanzaday and nawabzaday. It’s the same religious parties and same names, and either they win or their family members win. If they win, it is democracy, but if they don’t win, [the narrative is] there is dictatorship.”

On missing persons, he said the government had formed a commission to inquire into the matter. The DG ISPR added the commission had received just 10,901 applications since its formation in the early 2010s.

Of those, 9,372 cases had been disposed of, he said, adding that in 4,896 of the disposed-of cases, missing people had returned home, around 1,030 were located in prisons, 308 were found dead and 2,400 cases were declared as misreported cases.

Moreover, he said, 2,933 of the total cases were reported from Balochistan, among which 2, 767 had been disposed of.

He went on to say persons reported missing in the remaining cases were often found among killed terrorists after operations.

The DG ISPR added that terrorists were now also filming attacks to build a narrative that the situation in Balochistan was deteriorating.

He further pointed out that Balochistan’s area was 347,190 sq km, which was more than the area of many countries, as he elaborated on the need for more security personnel. He said this while speaking about raising a new command of the Frontier Corps, FC West, and its attached units in the province.

Sharing details of the current situation in Balochistan, he said terrorists had killed 178 civilians in the province this year, kidnapped 55 civilians, damaged roads and bridges at 24 places, set property on fire at 60 places and there were 47 incidents of looting.

Police and Levies were targeted in 105 incidents, he said.

They carry out terrorist activities, film it and release videos, and “elitists and sardarists start crying over the deteriorating situation”, he added. They target infrastructure and run this propaganda about a lack of development, the military’s spokesperson said, mentioning Indian involvement in such activities as well.

Here, he also spoke about the challenges faced by police as first responders, again citing Balochistan’s vast area as well as capacity constraints.

The DG ISPR further said that previous governments that let Levies be a “sardari force” were answerable in this regard. He questioned why the funds were not translated into equipment for police, adding, “Because you did not want to respond to your BLA pets.”

He then lauded police for fighting against terrorism, asking why were they not being acknowledged. “Because terrorists are making videos […] that are used to create a narrative,” he answered.

Moreover, he said terrorists were “honey-trapping” girls. They would kidnap and abuse them and then blackmail them into committing acts of terrorism.

He also said that 300 Indian websites were being operated for terrorism-related activities in Balochistan, more than 1,000 social media accounts were being used for the purpose and that a “hostile diaspora” was also involved in propaganda related to terrorism.

Explaining the social media ecosystem used by terrorists, the DG ISPR said: “First, an event or incident is seeded, right or wrong, and then it is framed by initiators, who hand it over to amplifiers. Then mass amplification is done by mainstream Indian media, channels and their print media as well, from where it is picked up by international media, and then you take it and run it as facts.”

Citing the example of the July 16 attack on a convoy in Mastung, the military spokesperson said that accounts associated with BYC, BLA and political parties based abroad were involved in amplifying it.

He further noted: “There is already an ecosystem here that whenever there is negative news about Pakistan, certain actors are always there to mark their attendance.”

Speaking of kinetic operations against terrorists in Balochistan, he said currently security forces were conducting Operation Shaban, which had been morphed into Operation Al-Azm.

He also said that most of the operations were carried out jointly by the army, FC and police.

Moreover, Operation Ghazab lil-Haq was also under way against the Afghan Taliban.

The military’s spokesperson said that 2.6 million Afghans had been repatriated to Afghanistan from Pakistan, of whom 600,000 were repatriated this year.

The general also said that work was underway to strengthen the capacity of security forces in the province, including the establishment of FC West in Chagai, which he said would ensure the “security of the mineral corridor”.

The DG ISPR added that the government was working on strengthening the police force as well, including the posting of newly recruited ASPs to Balochistan and the provision of bulletproof vehicles, among other measures.

He also stressed the significance of “empowering and appeasing” the common people of Balochistan. “We are committed to engaging and talking directly with people,” he said.

He added that Rs70 billion had been allocated to socioeconomic projects in Balochistan and Rs24bn for the Balochistan Special Development Initiative. He further stated that development projects aimed at improving road connectivity, IT training and human resources were also in progress.

Concluding his address, the DG ISPR played a video of the government’s direct engagements with people in Balochistan.

“This is the bright future of Balochistan that we need to further nurture, develop and propagate because Balochistan has a remarkable future,” he said.

“In the words of the Field Marshal, and he says it with a lot of conviction, within 5-10 years it is going to be the richest province; it is going to be a game changer. And the bigger the potential, the bigger the threats we face, but we, the people of Pakistan and Balochistan, will overcome [them].”

‘Kashmir jugular vein of Pakistan’

On the unrest in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), DG ISPR held, “Kashmir was, is and will remain a jugular vein of Pakistan.”

“Only one voice is coming from Pakistan: Kashmir will be Pakistan, and there is only one voice coming from Kashmir: Pakistan is ours, we are Pakistani, nothing can change that.”

Referring to the Joint Awami Action Committee’s (JAAC) protests, he said: “We knew who was behind that movement, but we wanted them to expose themselves. They have been exposed now.”

He said the JAAC opposed refugee representation in AJK’s legislature; however, the state had “wholeheartedly” asked them to contest the elections and approach the matter through legal and constitutional means.

“However, they want to pursue this by force, but only the state has the monopoly of violence.”

World.title: Pakistan welcomes Board of Peace developments under Gaza Peace Plan: PM Shehbaz
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday said that Pakistan welcomed developments under the Board of Peace towards implementing the disarmament process under the Gaza Peace Plan.

Earlier today, US President Donald Trump said talks in Cairo between mediators and Hamas leaders on Thursday have led to a phased disarmament agreement in Gaza, but a Hamas official described the deal as a draft and US officials said Israel was sceptical the Palestinian group would surrender its weapons.

“Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza,” Trump said in a social media post, adding that the disarmament would come in phases.

In a social media post on X, PM Shehbaz said, “Pakistan welcomes developments under the Board of Peace towards the implementation of the disarmament process under the Gaza Peace Plan.”

He emphasised that the mediating countries, including the United States of America, Egypt, Qatar and Turkiye, deserved “special appreciation for their efforts in achieving this progress”.

Commending President Trump’s “courageous leadership”, the premier said that this represented “a significant achievement for the Board of Peace”.

“Pakistan expresses the hope that with these developments, concrete steps will be taken towards implementing all commitments under the Gaza Peace Plan.

He concluded by expressing hope that these efforts would lead to the realisation of the right to self-determination of the Palestinian people through a credible and time-bound political process, in line with international legitimacy and relevant UN resolutions.

The prime minister added that this should result in the establishment of an independent, sovereign and contiguous State of Palestine based on the pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.

The board was initially proposed in September 2025 and formally established in January. Under its charter, the US government serves as its official depository and Trump has designated the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington as the Board’s headquarters.

A UN Security Council resolution adopted in mid-November last year authorised the board, along with cooperating states, to establish an international stabilisation force in Gaza following a ceasefire that began in October under a Trump-backed plan accepted by Israel and Hamas.

Pakistan is among the 14 countries that signed the charter of the Board of Peace on January 22 on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos, becoming a founding member of the body.

The list of founding members also includes Argentina, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Albania, Bahrain, Belarus, Bulgaria, Cambodia, El Salvador, Egypt, Hungary, Indonesia, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, Kuwait, Mongolia, Morocco, Paraguay, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam, spanning the Middle East, Asia, Europe, Latin America and the Caucasus.

The board was originally conceived to oversee the ceasefire and reconstruction of Gaza, but its charter expands its mandate to peace-building in all areas affected by or at risk of conflict.

World.title: Italy suspends Schengen agreement with Spain: foreign minister
World.content:
Italy has suspended its Schengen agreement with Spain, Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Friday, calling the measure “unavoidable”.

“The temporary suspension of Schengen with Spain is a necessary choice to safeguard the security of our citizens and defend the European borders,” he wrote in a post on X.

He noted that the influx of migrants in Ceuta, Spain, “reminds us that the management of the Union’s borders is a shared responsibility among our countries, one toward the other”.

“We must work together to prevent uncontrolled migrant flows from entering EU territory, with all the consequent risks and the threat of terrorism, which must be countered without hesitation,” he added.

US President Donald Trump led far-right attempts on Friday on both sides of the Atlantic to make political capital from Spain’s migration crisis, portraying the migrant surge in Ceuta as a warning for America if his opponents get into power.

“It’s terrible. Remember that picture. That’s going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in,” Trump was quoted as saying by Fox News. “If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life.”

With polls showing Trump’s support has fallen into the low 30 per cent range and opposition Democrats hoping to win at least partial control of Congress in November midterm elections, the crisis in Spain offers Republicans a chance to return to one of their political strongpoints.

News footage of migrants overwhelming barriers to get into Ceuta — a tiny Spanish territory on the Moroccan coast — aired repeatedly on Fox News and went viral across right-wing Trump-allied social media accounts.

In Europe, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel claimed in an X post that “Ceuta was left in ruins overnight” by the mass influx from Morocco. She argued that Germany is “likely the destination for most of these migrants”.

“Germany must prepare itself: borders must be secured and rejections rigorously enforced,” wrote Weidel, whose party is backed by top Trump officials.

Both Italy’s right-wing prime minister Giorgia Meloni and the populist right-wing ruling coalition in Finland called for excluding Spain from the European visa-free zone as a result of the situation.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a billionaire Trump supporter, said the Ceuta situation was caused by Spain’s policy of offering hundreds of thousands of migrants already in the country a legal status.

“They are replacing Spaniards with migrants,” Babis said.

‘Invasion of the West’

Trump’s election victory over Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 was fueled by voter worries over uncontrolled migration on the US-Mexico border and his lurid warnings of migrants coming to murder Americans and even to eat their pets.

Trump’s vice president, JD Vance, posted news footage on Friday of migrants pouring into Ceuta on X and wrote it highlighted “radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West.”

“These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration,” Vance posted on X.

Late on Thursday, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a chief architect of Trump’s anti-migration crackdown, posted video of the Ceuta crisis and said, “Democrats will see your home trampled and stolen by invaders and they will rejoice.”

World.title: Schools in Sindh to remain closed on August 4: education department
World.content:
The Sindh government’s School Education and Literacy Department on Friday announced that schools in the province would remain closed on Aug 4 (Tuesday) in observance of Chehlum of Imam Hussain (AS).

A notification available with Dawn states that all public and private educational institutions under the department “shall remain closed on Aug 4, 2026 (Tuesday) on account of Chehlum (20th Safar 1448 AH)”.

The notification has been sent to the principal secretaries of the Sindh governor and chief minister, as well as other senior officials.

The Chehlum of Imam Hussain is observed on Safar 20, highlighting the sacrifices rendered by Imam Husain (AS) and his companions in Karbala.

Earlier today, the department said private schools in Sindh have been allowed to decide their weekly teaching and working days according to their own schedules and convenience.

A circular issued by the province’s Directorate of Inspection and Registration of Private Institutions clarified a notification issued by the education department on July 29, which directed that classes would be held six days a week at schools and colleges across the province from August 1 until further notice.

The new circular clarified that the directive would not apply to privately managed schools.

World.title: Shangla mourns 28 miners killed in Balochistan coal mine accident
World.content:
SHANGLA: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Shangla district is mourning the deaths of 28 young coal miners, including 23 residents of Mian Kaly, who were killed in a gas explosion at a coal mine on the outskirts of Quetta on Thursday.

The Shangla Coal Mine Workers Association said that following the deaths of 23 miners from Mian Kaly, almost every household in the village was mourning the loss of a family member.

Abid Yaar, president of the Shangla Coal Mine Workers Association, said that Mian Kaly had become the epicentre of repeated coal mine tragedies.

“A total of 28 deceased workers were from Shangla district — 23 from Mian Kaly (Pir Abad), two from Kana, and one each from Bada and Gata Bely Baba,” he said.

He added that the victims, aged between 17 and 25, belonged to the same families and were cousins or close relatives. According to Yaar, several of the deceased were orphans whose fathers had also lost their lives in previous coal mine accidents.

He alleged that the tragedy resulted from the mine administration’s negligence and the absence of essential safety measures, claiming that there was no proper ventilation system in the government-run mine, which led to the deadly gas explosion.

“It is not just an accident but a lifelong trauma for the families, orphans, widows and mothers who lost their loved ones. These young men had gone there only to earn a livelihood and support their families back home,” Yaar said.

Responding to a question, he noted that Shangla lacked factories and other opportunities for skilled employment, forcing young people to work in hazardous coal mines and risk their lives to make ends meet.

The victims’ family members criticised the government for not arranging ambulances to transport their loved ones’ bodies, adding that they had to bring the remains in a van at their own expense.

According to the Shangla administration, one body arrived on Friday evening, with the others expected to arrive later at night and early on Saturday morning.

Three of the miners who lost their lives in the tragedy were brothers.

Earlier today, rescue teams recovered 32 bodies overnight from two coal mines in the Sorange coalfield near Quetta after a methane gas explosion, while the search for two more miners was underway.

The explosion occurred on Thursday at a private coal mine in the Sorange coalfield, about 30 kilometres northeast of Quetta. The methane gas explosion triggered a fire, caused the mine to collapse, and affected another nearby mine.

Chief Inspector of Mines Balochistan Muhammad Atif told Dawn that 34 miners were inside the two mines when the explosion occurred.

“So far, 32 bodies have been recovered from both mines,” he said. “The operation is continuing in the mine where the explosion took place to recover two miners.”

The explosion severely affected another mine near the main site, with 12 miners working in the second mine at the time.

In June, at least three people were injured after explosive material used in mining accidentally detonated in the Khanuzai area.

In April, at least five coal miners were killed in two separate mine accidents that took place in the Bolan and Duki coalfield areas of Balochistan.

World.title: Private schools in Sindh to decide weekly working days at their own convenience, education department says
World.content:
All private schools in Sindh have been allowed to decide their weekly teaching and working days according to their own schedules and convenience, the Sindh Education and Literacy Department said on Friday.

A circular issued by the province’s Directorate of Inspection and Registration of Private Institutions clarified a notification issued by the education department on July 29, which directed that classes would be held six days a week at schools and colleges across the province from August 1 until further notice.

The new circular clarified that the directive would not apply to privately managed schools.

“It is hereby clarified for all privately managed schools across the province of Sindh that they may manage their weekly working days according to their own schedules and operative convenience,” Additional Director (Registration) Rafia Javed said in the circular.

A copy of the circular is available with Dawn.

In its July 29 notification, seen by Dawn, the Education and Literacy Department said: “In supercession of this department’s notification of even number dated March 31, 2026, it is hereby notified that all public and private educational institutions under the administrative control of the School and Literacy Education Department, Government of Sindh, shall observe a six-day working week (Monday to Saturday) with effect from August 1, 2026 till further orders.”

The College Education Department issued its own version of the notification a day later, directing that a six-day working week be observed by all public and private educational institutions under its administrative control.

On March 31, as cited in the two notifications, the Sindh government had announced that Saturday and Sunday would be “off” days at educational institutions, as part of the austerity and fuel conservation measures adopted to deal with the economic impact of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

The Sindh chief minister’s spokesperson, however, told Dawn that teachers had also stopped working on Saturdays, although the March decision applied only to students. He said this had affected students’ education and the completion of the annual curriculum. The six-day week was introduced to facilitate completion of the curriculum.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.
