He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Farmer posts reward after dog shot at family nursery
World.content:
A north-east Victorian farmer is offering a $20,000 reward after his family dog was shot in a suspected drive-by attack.

Tom Powell was driving an all-terrain vehicle at his plant nursery in Stanley, near Beechworth, when his German short-haired pointer, Daisy, was shot just metres from where he was driving.

The dog was running with eight other family dogs before the incident around 8:40am on May 15.

Two staff members were also on site nearby weeding garlic.

Mr Powell said Daisy survived the shooting; the bullet entered her rear leg and exited her abdomen.

Daisy was fortunate to recover from her bullet wounds. (Supplied: Tom Powell)

The beloved family pet is recovering well having received around $2,700 worth of veterinary care.

The family initially offered a $5,000 reward for information leading to conviction, and has since ramped up the offering due to concerns about community safety.

"$20,000 is not actually a lot when you're talking about people's lives; it's quite a small amount actually," Mr Powell said.

Daisy is at home recovering from her injuries. (Supplied: Tom Powell)

"Daisy was shot, but what if that was one of my boys — they're 25, 30 years old, working here all the time, our grandchildren, staff, customers.

" It's not a lot, but it may get people talking and might make a difference. "

Mr Powell said he has lodged a police report and that an investigation is underway, but that no leads had been uncovered.

He said he was convinced the shooting was deliberate after the family was subject to a string of complaints over the past decade in relation to the business.

"There's no consequences for people's actions anymore, and it's probably taking advantage of that … and just people trying to scare us and Daisy got shot."

Stanley is a popular town for families to visit orchards in north-east Victoria. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

Mr Powell said he believed she was shot by a person driving by the nursery on Stanley Road.

The family previously successfully turned to social media around four years ago when $20,000 worth of bikes and tools were stolen from their property.

They offered a $10,000 reward, with the community call-out generating important information, Mr Powell said.

Victoria Police has been contacted for comment.

World.title: How Gen Z sees money — and how it drives their spending and saving
World.content:
Liam* was never taught how to manage money.

So, when he earned his first pay cheque at 16, keeping it was a challenge.

His purchases started small — treating himself to things he'd gone without growing up, like a steak at a restaurant.

Then the habits escalated — gaming consoles, online spending, takeaway.

His pay started to only last days.

"Tapping my card felt too easy because I never actually saw the money leaving my hand," he said.

Growing up in a financially unstable household where money was uncertain and rarely discussed, Liam entered adulthood without learning basic skills like budgeting or saving.

Watching his pay disappear reminded him of the instability he experienced as a child, when his financial security depended on someone else's decisions.

He realised he was repeating the pattern.

Liam spent the next six months consciously changing his habits, and by the end of it, he had almost $10,000 in the bank.

Gen Z savers, against the odds

Liam isn't alone.

Data from the NAB Wellbeing Survey Q1 2026 found young Australians aged 18-29 have the highest saving intention compared to older age groups.

In total, 94 per cent of Gen Z women were trying to save compared to 93 per cent for Gen Z men.

Both sat above the 81 per cent national average of all Australians putting money aside.

But Gen Z are also navigating a financial world that looks very different from previous generations — shaped by tap-and-go payments, buy now, pay later services, online ads and an endless stream of financial advice online.

So, how are young people managing their money?

To find out, we spoke to a few.

Hugo's parents gave him the freedom to manage his own money, but still encouraged him to save. (ABC News: Marc Eiden)

Hugo, 16. Supermarket worker.

Hugo works part-time at a supermarket and spends most of his pay on car modifications.

His understanding of money came from learning through trial and error.

"I sort of just started saving after realising I had no money left," he said.

His parents encouraged saving but left him to manage it. Hugo said he's better with money now but uncertain about the future.

" I don't feel 100 per cent confident I'll buy a house, but I'm hopeful. "

Bree says she feels confident managing her money because she has strong influences and support around her. (ABC News: Dimitria Panagiotaros)

Bree, 16. Fast food worker.

Bree spends most of her income on phone data and food, with the occasional splurge on music or gifts. She's saving for a car.

"I only spend what I know I can afford based on my shifts," she said.

Her parents taught her to budget using their own financial books.

"They really wanted us to learn from their mistakes."

Her mum can view her bank account but doesn't control it. She hopes to buy a house one day, though she worries about the current market.

Evelynn says whenever she has money, her mum reminds her not to blow it all. (ABC News: Amber Irving-Guthrie)

Evelynn, 16. Cello busker.

Evelynn earns money busking and spends most of it on social outings with friends.

She has her own bank account, but is still figuring out how to manage it.

"I feel like managing money is really stressful. I don't think most kids are very well educated on money," she said.

Evelynn has searched for advice online, like, 'How do I save money faster?' but felt she "never got a good answer on that".

When financial education falls short

Behind those different experiences is a common factor: not every young person starts with the same financial education or support.

Alyssia Kennedy, 29, runs the Life After School program, visiting Tasmanian high schools to teach students the practical money skills they're not getting in the classroom or at home, including tax, work rights and budgeting.

She said the demand told its own story.

"So many schools are reaching out saying, 'We need your help because we as teachers don't know these things either.'"

Ms Kennedy said the gap was generational.

Alyssia Kennedy founded the Life After School program to bridge educational gaps. (ABC News: Audrey Courty)

"People in their 50s and 60s were taught this, whether it was by mum and dad or through school," she said.

"But the curriculum has changed a lot since then. I'm seeing gaps with those whose parents are in their 40s or under."

"Some parents want to know how to have these conversations, while others don't have the knowledge themselves."

Ms Kennedy said what young people were spending on had not changed dramatically, but what had changed was their ability to access those things, making it easier than ever to spend without registering the cost.

Where Gen Z are getting their advice

When financial education is inconsistent, many young people are turning elsewhere for guidance.

The ASIC Moneysmart Gen Z Financial Behaviours Report 2026 found that 63 per cent of Gen Z use social media for financial guidance, while 52 per cent trust 'finfluencers' and 64 per cent trust AI platforms.

Nearly one in four own cryptocurrencies, with 29 per cent saying they trade based on social media or influencer recommendations.

Still, the data doesn't paint Gen Z as careless with money.

Sixty per cent also use professional sources for financial advice, while half turn to family and friends.

The findings suggest Gen Z is actively seeking financial information, but doing so through unregulated digital platforms, where algorithms can shape the content they see.

Nearly three in four Gen Z Australians saw ads encouraging cryptocurrency investment, while more than four in 10 were contacted directly by someone offering investment advice. (Adobe Stock)

Figuring it out anyway

For Liam, now 17, changing his financial habits meant rethinking his relationship with money.

He decided to put most of his pay aside in cash, limiting his access to digital spending. He cooked cheap meals and repaired things instead of replacing them.

"I realised that if I put a majority of it away in cash, it built up really quickly," he said.

For a generation raised on digital payments, tap and go has made spending faster and more convenient. (AAP: Dan Peled)

The almost $10,000 he saved bought a car, paid for a holiday, and helped him move out of home, things he said once felt out of reach.

Liam's story is one example of how Gen Z is learning how to manage money in a financial landscape unlike previous generations.

*Liam's name has been changed..

World.title: FIFA executive lashes Infantino over sell-off plan
World.content:
FIFA's chief operating officer said its staff were deceived by president Gianni Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan, and suggested the project must not go ahead.

Zurich-based executive Kevin Lamour all but invited Infantino to fire him in a statement to the Associated Press that defended his colleagues amid intense fallout from the FIFA boss's plan to sell stakes in future World Cup profits to private equity funds.

Lamour wrote that staff were "deceived" by Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

"It is the project of one person," wrote Lamour, a long-time colleague of Infantino at both FIFA and European soccer body UEFA.

Gianni Infantino (left) and Donald Trump were often seen together during and in the lead-up to the 2026 World Cup. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill)

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Lamour's statement came hours after Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Cordeiro wrote in a statement. The former US Soccer Federation president said he was not included in talks about the plan backed by a New York investment fund created by Joshua Kushner.

"Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," Cordeiro said. He called the $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) commercial subsidiary "a bad deal for football".

Lamour did not resign the post he has held since 2024 but said he had a duty to his colleagues.

Joshua Kushner (right, pictured with brother Jared, left) is leading the charge to make a private investment in FIFA. (Getty Images: Patrick McMullan)

"And if that means I lose my job then so be it," the French official said.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Lamour came to soccer from politics two decades ago as an aide to then-UEFA president Michel Platini. He often had an international role in soccer politics liaising with FIFA member federations in Africa and Asia, who are weighing their own decisions about Infantino's offers of $US20 million each by a deadline of September 19.

Cordeiro often joined Infantino on working visits to meet US President Donald Trump at the White House in recent years.

"Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away," he said.

"That is why this proposal should be rejected."

Infantino has proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor," described by FIFA, is Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

"FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organisation sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt," Cordeiro said. He noted FIFA's revenue of $15 billion in the past four years tied to the men's World Cup just ended.

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification," he said.

Cordeiro said he shared five years of working for FIFA alongside Infantino with "dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game".

"I hope they, too, will speak up," he wrote, "because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."

Infantino has been president of FIFA for more than 10 years and seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next March. FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for challengers to come forward.

Lamour was part of Infantino's inner circle that campaigned for him to become the surprise winner of that FIFA presidential election in February 2016.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Mothers turn maternity leave side hustle into beloved community pantry
World.content:
The biting cold of a winter morning in Guyra, northern NSW, doesn't keep new mothers Tash Cunningham and Eowyn Lacey from rugging up their little ones and heading down to the Bus Shelter Pantry.

What was meant to be a maternity leave passion project, selling their excess farm and garden produce, has grown into a micro bakery.

Dozens of people stop to enjoy baked sweets, jams, and fruit and vegetables all made and grown by the mothers

With all their ingredients being self-sustainable, the mothers easily cover the small costs of running the operation.

"It stemmed from a love for self-sustainability," Ms Cunningham said.

"We both wanted to be self-sufficient.

Loading...

"We were both about to be on maternity leave, and we thought, 'That gives us six to 12 months, do we just have a go?'"

Ms Lacey said they both wanted farm stalls.

"It was just one of those dreams we had floating around," she said.

"I'm a really big gardener, I always have excess veggies I can't use."

The mums started the pantry, with two cartons of eggs, five zucchinis, a couple of punnets of cherry tomatoes, and some muffins.

Now their shelves and fridges are loaded.

The pantry has several shelves and fridges loaded with goodies. (ABC New England: Peter Sanders)

"I'll come down most days to stock up, and its nothing for me to meet two or three people in the five minutes I'm here," Ms Cunningham said.

" People leave the highway just to come and see, and they're walking away with an armful of things … you wouldn't believe the fridge would empty, but it does. "

The home-baked sweets have become a hit with the customers. (Supplied: Bus Stop Pantry)

Ms Lacey said the enterprise had turned into "pretty much a full-time business".

"I need employees at this point," she said.

"I do all my cooking after [my daughter] goes to bed … I've coming in at 11 at night to fill up the fridges."

Community inspiration

The work the women put into running the Bus Shelter Pantry is a labour of love for the wider Guyra community.

"Being homemade, I think, is the biggest thing [for the community]," Ms Cunningham said.

"We've had people tell us that they really appreciate the nostalgia of the recipes.

"We're not trying to reinvent the wheel; they are just genuine older recipes people love."

The Bus Shelter Pantry sells all sorts of different items. (ABC New England: Peter Sanders)

Their work has inspired others to get into self-sustainability, with some even asking if they could sell their homemade products at the pantry.

"A fella's daughter makes crochet, and he makes all the jams, they're very artistic and the jams are delicious," Ms Lacey said.

"The people who supply the honey are local bee keepers out near Tingha."

Community-made crafts are also sold. (ABC New England: Peter Sanders)

The mothers encourage locals to get into sustainable food, believing locally grown and supplied food is the right direction for food security.

"We all get so confident going to the supermarket that food is going to be there," Ms Cunningham said.

" But there is no guarantee, I don't think people realised the trucks could have stopped not too long ago with the cost of fuel. "

Leaving a legacy

As the women's children continue to grow, and the mothers approach the end of their maternity leave, it remains to be seen how the Bus Shelter Pantry will continue to run.

"We've got some big dreams where we'd like to take it, with getting solar power, so it could keep going," Ms Cunningham said.

"I'm trying to wonder if I could fit it all in, I don't need sleep anymore," Ms Lacey joked.

Tash Cunningham wants her children Allora and Myles to learn to be self-sustainable. (ABC New England: Peter Sanders)

Ultimately, the biggest success of the pantry is the legacy it leaves for their children.

"Showing them how to grow their own vegetables, make there own bread, be a bit self-sufficient, these are skills that kids are not raised with anymore," Ms Cunningham said.

Eowyn Lacey cannot wait to share her love of plants with Kyindy. (ABC New England: Peter Sanders)

"I can't wait to teach [my daughter] about plants … pass on some skills I spent years developing," Ms Lacey said.

Even if the Bus Shelter Pantry does close down, the children will still have a homemade bus shelter to use on their trips to school.

The Bus Shelter Pantry will remain a legacy for the next generation. (ABC New England: Peter Sanders)

"It just might be a bus shelter with sweets in the back, to help them be popular at school," Ms Cunningham said.

World.title: Lewis 'not surprised' no-one shook Comm Games 200m champion's hand
World.content:
Australian sprint star Torrie Lewis says she is not surprised no-one embraced gold medallist Adaejah Hodge after the women's 200m final.

Lewis finished sixth in her pet event after something of a surprise bronze in the 100m final a few nights prior.

The 21-year-old won her semifinal and was one of the fastest qualifiers into Friday's final, local time, where she was drawn alongside Hodge, who broke the Commonwealth Games record in the semis.

Hodge stormed to gold in 22.07 seconds, but the customary hugs and embraces between competitors were absent.

"Let's just say I'm not surprised no-one shook her hand and I'm not supposed to say any more than that," Lewis said.

Torrie Lewis was told not to talk about Adaejah Hodge. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

She added: "I've been told not to say anything. I would love to say some words, but I'm not allowed to.

"I think everyone knows what I would like to say, but just fill in the blank yourself."

If you are slightly confused, the context goes back to 2024.

Hodge, from the British Virgin Islands, tested positive for a banned substance from a sample given at the under-20 world championships in 2024, where she won the 200m ahead of Lewis on August 30 in Lima.

Hodge tested positive for banned metabolic modulator GW1516, also known as Cardarine or Endurobol, which increases fat metabolism and improves exercise adaptation, according to Sport Integrity Australia.

Lewis was elevated to the gold-medal position when Hodge was banned in March 2025, with the Australian celebrating being "the 1st clean runner across the line" on Instagram.

Loading Instagram content

The findings from an Athletics Integrity Unit investigation at the time revealed that Hodge was told about the positive test in November and she gave "an explanation" and "additional information" that convinced investigators she accidentally (on the balance of probabilities) ingested the substance.

Hodge's explanation and "substantial assistance" in the case meant what would have been a two-year ban, taking her through to August 27 this year, was reduced by seven months, allowing her to resume competing in January and make it to Glasgow.

Both runners received automatic places in the semifinals of the 200m, with Lewis winning the first race in 22.64 and Hodge running a Games record of 22.01 to win hers, setting up their first rematch since that infamous race in Peru two years ago.

Hodge said she came out with a point to prove.

Adaejah Hodge's doping ban was reduced by seven months for her cooperation with the investigation, allowing her to comepte in Glasgow. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I've put all that behind me. I just wanted [to] move forward and work extra hard to show I didn't need it. I never will need it," she said.

"I just knew I had to put in extra work to prove to the people, the haters, that I'm Adaejah Hodge."

And she was unfazed by the lack of connection with her rivals.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

"It's competition. Everybody's goal out here is to win. I don't really know what to say about that," she said.

"It's about competing, and if you wanna shake my hand, you wanna shake my hand. If you don't, you don't. I'm gonna be a good sport, I'm gonna tell everybody good job because we all put in the hard work to be out here and compete to the highest level."

As for Lewis and the rest of the field.

"This is my first time meeting some of the girls, but they all seem really nice," she said.

World.title: Chaos vs calm: What to expect when Australia and Ireland go head-to-head
World.content:
Last year, when the AFL reached out to the Irish players in the AFLW to gauge their interest in a representative game, it was a resounding yes please.

"Everyone was screaming yes, being like, 'Let's do it,' we wanted this for so long," GWS star EIlish O'Dowd told ABC Sport.

"We're so delighted that it's been put in place … It's hard to tell how it's going to be."

The inaugural clash between Australia and Ireland was officially announced in May, with plans for it organised quickly.

The players were offered a Gaelic ball or Sherrin to play with, with the Irish contingent opting for the latter and playing under Australian Rules.

Irish fans of AFLW These Irish families get up at all hours of the night to watch AFLW and host viewing parties with 30-plus people for big games.

Irish captain Orla O'Dwyer joked that if they had chosen the sphere ball used in Ireland, the Australian girls would just get "hammered".

"(But) having the top Irish and Aussie players come together and play, I suppose that's why we're here, we're here to play AFLW, that's why we got drafted, that's why we came," O'Dwyer said.

"You might have Irish fans go to this game to support Ireland, and they might leave being AFLW fans for the season, and that's huge as well for the growth of our game."

Irish players are known to be fast, and at times, chaotic. There is more running with constant play in Gaelic football.

Vikki Wall of Ireland is tackled by Ash Riddell of Australia during yesterday's captain's run. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

Given the short turnaround time to get the marquee game going, including players going into camp just days ago with not even a main training afforded, the styles of play expected are the chaos of the Irish versus the composure of AFLW under North Melbourne's Darren Crocker.

The Irish coach, also Sydney's new head coach, Colin O'Riordan, joked at the pre-match press conference he did not want to "give away all the secrets that we don't have".

"You just have to adapt and overcome. That's the mentality probably. (And) speaking from an Irish person, that's a lot of our mentality as Irish people is adapt and overcome," O'Riordan said.

"We haven't had a main training session; we'll do a captain's run today, but at the same time, does that really matter? Probably not. It just forces us to come together quicker."

Crocker said his Australian side had the chance to come together and speak about their identity for the clash.

He gestured to Australian captain Jasmine Garner, also the captain under him at the Kangaroos. "If you look at the person sitting next to me, just so skilful, great decision maker, really composed, really calm," he said.

"I think we've got a really well-balanced team in regards to that. Colin's mentioned the word chaos … I feel like it could be a little bit of composure and control against chaos.

"You know, that sounded quite like a Get Smart episode!"

Fans turned out to opening training for pictures and signatures from the AFLW players. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

He added that it would be a mistake to underestimate what this game means for both sides.

"It is a great honour to be the first to play a historic AFLW international game against Ireland. It's fantastic and a real privilege for us. I hope the Irish aren't underestimating how patriotic the Australians are as well," he said.

Fans are keen to see particular match-ups, especially between players from the same team, such as O'Dwyer and her Brisbane teammate and Australian representative Sophie Conway on the wing.

They'll see a lot of players rotating through the game.

The game being on the eve of the upcoming season, just one week before the season opener at Docklands Stadium between Carlton and St Kilda, means there are some concerns about workload and conditioning.

To manage these physical demands, both teams will use an extended nine-player interchange bench (four more than in standard AFLW matches).

"There are (some players on managed minutes), but that's the beauty of having nine players on the interchange. We can give this experience to all 25 players, knowing that a few of them are being load managed. … It allows those players to experience this," Crocker said.

There are 46 current Irish players across the AFLW competition. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

There are 46 Irish players across the competition. A lot of big-name stars will feature in today's clash against Australia, such as Sarah Rowe, Vikki Wall, Áine McDonagh, Niamh McLaughlin, Erika O'Shea, Dayna Finn and Aishling Moloney, while some lesser-known names also got the call-up to fill out the squad.

Meanwhile, Australia had almost 500 players to pick from, meaning Crocker's side could pull from a much larger pool of All Australians, premiership players and best and fairests, with each selection known across the competition as a star player.

For this reason, and playing under Australian Rules, O'Dwyer said she is fine with the Irish not going in as favourites.

"Us Irish, we love being an underdog, it's something we thrive off of," she said.

World.title: Details of ransom notes in Nancy Guthrie case released
World.content:
Authorities in the United States have released an early ransom note in the investigation into the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie, in hopes that someone will recognise the writing style.

A second note released Friday, local time, indicated the 84-year-old died shortly after she was kidnapped.

Both notes initially went to a Tucson television station days after the mother of Today show co-host Savannah Guthrie went missing from her home outside Tucson on February 1.

TV host's fresh plea for mother's whereabouts The US TV show host Savannah Guthrie makes another plea to her mother's kidnappers.

Authorities have not said whether Nancy Guthrie is still alive.

The Pima County Sheriff's Department said "we believe these distinctive linguistic characteristics may be recognisable to someone who knows or has interacted with the notes' writer".

The first note, sent February 2, said Nancy was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $US4 million ($5.68 million) in cryptocurrency, with the ransom amount increasing if the first demand was not met.

It said Nancy would be released within 12 hours if the payment was received. It also included a threat to kill her if the ransom wasn't paid.

"Your mother is aware of this and her life is in your hands," the first note read.

"It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible."

The second note to the family said Nancy died shortly after she was taken.

"She is buried in nature now," the second note said.

"Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome."

The note ends with an apology, "We are truly sorry."

The sheriff's department said the notes reveal a distinctive pattern of word choices and provide insight into the writer's mindset. The agency said someone who knows the notes' writer may recognise the patterns.

In a statement, the sheriff's department also went further to appeal to people who may know something about the case, saying it may be difficult to come forward due to a personal relationship with someone involved or just for their own safety.

"We recognise relationships and loyalties change over time, as do people and their perspectives," the sheriff's department wrote.

"It is not too late to come forward."

Daughter Savannah Guthrie made an emotional appeal in a social media post earlier this week. (Reuters: @savannahguthrie via Instagram)

Despite an intense search involving thousands of law enforcement officers and volunteers, there has been no sign of the mother of three since she was reported missing.

Her children, including the NBC host, have made heartbreaking video pleas for help, but to no avail.

On Monday, Savannah Guthrie made a fresh plea to her mother's kidnappers.

"I’m asking you, begging you, to do the right thing now. Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her. I truly believe it is never too late to do the right thing,” she said.

The sheriff's office said: “Investigators continue to pursue every available technological and investigative lead. However, community members remain a vital resource as we seek to provide answers for Nancy’s family.”

AP

World.title: Gym owner fighting for insurance nearly four years after 2022 floods
World.content:
Nearly four years after parts of Victoria were devastated by the 2022 floods, a small business in central Victoria is still locked in a battle with its insurer.

Adam and Alex Griffiths' gym was one of six businesses on the same street in Seymour without flood cover.

Adam Griffiths in the floodwater inside his gym on October 14, 2022. (Supplied: Adam Griffiths)

They were all initially rejected for storm cover, but five had the decision overturned by their insurers, who accepted that stormwater inundated the businesses before the river flood arrived.

Only the Griffiths' insurer, Hollard, has maintained its denial.

"All I needed to do was partner with some other insurer, and I would have been covered," Mr Griffiths said.

"It's very disappointing that the company can sit there and watch the damage and devastation — it's my livelihood and my staff's livelihood — and they can just say no."

Record rainfall

As rain fell in the morning of October 13, 2022, fitness classes were running as normal in the gym.

But Mr Griffiths said there were signs of what was coming as water filled the street and crept up his car park.

"I ended up calling the police and closing the street down, after that all we could do was pretty much sandbag," he said.

Alex and Adam Griffiths with their dogs inside their Seymour gym. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Mr Griffiths said stormwater inundated the gym in the afternoon, damaging the floors and equipment, well before floodwaters arrived.

The Goulburn River at Seymour peaked in the early hours of the next morning at 8.26 metres, marking the town's worst flood in more than 100 years.

Wallis Street at 6.50pm on October 13, 2022, looking towards the Goulburn River. (Supplied: Courtney Carroll)

Hollard declined an interview with the ABC, but a spokesperson said the company engaged an expert hydrologist to review all the information supplied by Mr Griffiths, "with the findings supporting the original claim decision".

"We will continue to work with the customer and their representative should they wish to provide any additional information or seek further review from AFCA," the spokesperson said.

To rebuild the gym without the help of insurance, Mr Griffiths worked a second job in sales.

'Ridiculous' situation

Courtney Carroll owns the Stihl Shop two doors down and said the street was "like a lake" at about 10am on October 13.

Water flooded the car park outside the Stihl Shop on Wallis Street. (Supplied: Courtney Carroll)

"[The water] was in our business around 5pm to 6pm and then the flood didn't come through until later that night or early the next morning," she said.

Her stormwater inundation claim for the business was originally denied, but later overturned.

"We're all 45 Wallis Street. How do [units] 1, 2, 3 and 5 get an inundation claim and not 4?" she said.

"We're not denying we were flooded, but we were definitely inundated with water from the gutters … which we proved."

Shaun McCormick has relocated his business from Wallis Street since the floods. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Another neighbouring business owner, Shaun McCormick, said the situation facing Mr Griffiths was "ridiculous".

"It should've been dealt with years ago, and more should've been done to help him," he said.

Experts disagree

Seymour-based insurance consultant TR Keller has acted on behalf of the six businesses.

He said one of the issues highlighted in the federal inquiry into insurers' responses to 2022 major floods was the reliance of insurers on expert reports without interrogating the evidence themselves.

The gym sandbagged to try to prevent water damage. (Supplied: Adam Griffiths)

"We had overwhelmingly additional and compelling evidence to show that it is stormwater, " he said.

"But yet [Hollard's] expert is … sticking to their guns and saying it's all floodwater. And the insurer says, 'that's what our expert says, we can't do anything about it.'"

The Australian Financial Complaints Authority upheld Hollard's refusal last year.

It found there was insufficient evidence to establish stormwater alone was capable of causing damage to the property.

Mr Griffiths hopes the evidence of a third hydrologist supporting his claim will be enough to reopen the complaint and overturn the decision.

"It starts to become almost energy-sapping to always hear no, especially when you feel like you're in the right," he said.

"We'll do whatever we can."

World.title: Dan Gorringe was a battling ruckman. He’s now a social media star and might even become an AFL rights holder
World.content:
Gorringe is edgy, but even the AFL wants him.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you’re a football fan under the age of 35, chances are Dan Gorringe is everywhere when you pick up your phone. Log on to Instagram, he’ll be there, over-celebrating a Carlton win or mourning a loss. You’ll find his mildly more serious football views on his Dan Does Footy YouTube channel. On TikTok, you’ll get his almost instant hot takes, delivered in his typically edgy style. Dan Does Footy podcast host and social media identity Daniel Gorringe has become a key player in the AFL’s targeting of the youth market. Chris Hopkins He’s labelled goalkicking great Matthew Lloyd a “dirty rat”, called prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley a “muppet”, and told arguably the greatest player of all time Leigh Matthews to “f--- up”. He has had commercial partnerships with corporate bookies, sports drinks and alcohol brands. It will come as a surprise, then, that Gorringe the footballer was the polar opposite in personality. “He was as straight as six o’clock,” his first senior coach Guy McKenna said. Former Carlton captain and one of Gorringe’s closest friends Sam Docherty, who was unwittingly embroiled in his stoush with Whateley, said his former teammate was rarely the centre of attention in the Blues locker room.



“He was fairly quiet, [but] still very funny,” Docherty said. “If you listen to him speak, he’s probably socially anxious and awkward through footy because he didn’t know where he stood or what he was doing. He always had that funny side to him. “He joked around with a small group of mates as opposed to the whole locker room. Most people who played with him would have thought he was fairly reserved and didn’t speak very much.” Dan Gorringe takes on North Melbourne’s Todd Goldstein in a ruck contest in 2016. Getty Images In many ways, Gorringe is the most unlikely of football personalities: polarising, unfiltered and contemptuous of traditional media. But even the AFL wants him. Traditionally, it has taken a long and distinguished on-field career for a retired player to make it in the media. Though a No.10 pick in 2010, his 26 games for Gold Coast and Carlton fall well short of the mark. As a player, his most memorable moment came in retirement when he clattered into comedian Dave Hughes in a legends charity match. But the world of social media does not follow the same rules, and there are few in Australian sport better at playing this game than Gorringe, who has a team of more than 10 full-timers and additional casual and part-time staff behind the scenes managing content and his commercial partnerships. His success is no accident.



The former ruckman has a greater digital presence than some clubs. His 378,000 followers on Instagram is well over double that of Gold Coast, the club that drafted him. His 43,200 subscribers on YouTube is close to 50 per cent higher than another of his former teams, Carlton, and his TikTok following of 298,000 is more than the Blues and Suns combined. His average of more than 300,000 views and 20,000-plus engagements per content item across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube makes him “one of Australia’s highest-performing independent sports creator brands”, Nathan Powell, the chief product and strategy officer at AI-powered creator technology platform Fabulate, said. “Dan has managed to build something that’s much harder than simply accumulating followers,” Powell said. AFL CEO Andrew Dillon with influencer Dan Gorringe, announcing the league’s first official watchalong. AFL “He’s built a highly concentrated Australian sporting audience that consistently chooses to engage with his content. The audience is also predominantly male and heavily concentrated in the 18-to-34 demographic, which is one of the most valuable audiences for sporting organisations and advertisers. “That tells me people aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.” No wonder the AFL has Gorringe on its books as part of what its customer and commercial boss Bec Haagsma says is a “rapid transformation and evolution of our fan engagement and fan experience strategy”. They see Gorringe as pivotal to targeting the younger market – those under the age of 34.



In collaboration with the league’s broadcast partners, Gorringe appeared on The Ultimate Footy Watchalong for the Fremantle v Sydney and North Melbourne v Melbourne games, streamed live on the AFL’s YouTube channel, Kayo and 7plus. “Watchalongs”, where fans stream themselves watching a game live and connect online in real time, are a new concept in Australia and, if experience overseas is any indication, here to stay. “It goes back to the idea that media is changing, and social media is a massive part of the media industry,” Michael Neill, the head of Fox Footy, said. “It won’t get any smaller. We’d be foolish if we didn’t look at these new ideas and different ways to broadcast. “The immediacy of his posts and how he gets his opinion out there really quick, it’s out there and it’s different. “It comes from an ex-player’s perspective as well, and from someone who’s very smart when it comes to communication and how to get his message out there.” For Seven, it gives the network another way to reach the younger market.



“Working with creators who love the game allows us to connect with audiences in authentic new ways,” Seven’s head of sport digital Kirsty Bradmore said. “We are continually exploring more ways to innovate our broadcast offering for viewers across Australia.” This collaboration drew 250,000 live viewers across the league’s YouTube channel, Kayo, Foxtel and 7plus to watch while Gorringe and co-hosts – Seven reporter Xander McGuire and Collingwood AFLW captain and Kayo personality Ruby Schleicher – casually discussed the game, as opposed to the serious analysis on the main coverage. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach, a GWS fan, featured at half-time. ‘People aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.’ Nathan Powell of creator technology platform Fabulate “Dan has been with us for a year now doing some hardcore engagement stuff,” Haagsma said. “He’s part of that strategy. For us, looking at how we attract, retain and engage with our avid fans is a different proposition to our younger fans. “We knew we needed to engage a different strategy. We can’t put highlights on TikTok and go, ‘That will bring the kids in’. Dan has got a voice that we know speaks in a different way, and just resonates. He’s authentic in his point of view, and he loves the game.” Gorringe’s channel markets itself as “unfiltered and unqualified”. The wider football community saw this side in March after he aired a voice memo left by Docherty of a candid and expletive-laden analysis of his former club’s failings in their thumping by Sydney on the opening night of the season. Gorringe did not check with Docherty if the message was to be aired, as is the practice in mainstream media, drawing condemnation from Whateley – who slammed him for “reprehensible behaviour”.

World.title: Knock on wood, but I think I’ve wasted enough time on silly superstitions
World.content:
August 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We were sitting outside in the sun, on the broad steps of Sydney’s new fish market, when a bird flew overhead and launched a massive poo on the young woman sitting in front of us. The “dropping” was enormously accurate and voluminous, covering all of her left hand, part of her left arm and much of her dress. Keen to make her feel better, I told her: “They say it brings good luck.” What’s so bad about a black cat? Getty Images Her boyfriend turned with a smile. “In that case,” he says, “she’s in for a lot of good luck. Heaps of it.” At which point he began helping with the laborious clean-up. What are the origins of these superstitions? Who was the first person to see someone cop a flying splodge of bird poo, and then say: “They say it brings good luck”?



I understand the principle: something unfortunate has happened, so you want to make the person feel better. But why bird poo? We don’t offer this consolation after other misfortunes. If someone smacks their head into a low-lying branch, we don’t say: “Lucky dog! You better buy a lottery ticket.” If you get mugged, the thief pushing you to the ground and stealing your phone, the next person along doesn’t help you to your feet with the cheery observation: “Well, there’s nothing like a violent mugging to bring a bit of good luck.” Most superstitions make no sense. Why does a rabbit foot bring great fortune? It certainly didn’t work for the rabbit from which it was removed. And what’s so bad about a black cat? You wouldn’t dream of judging a person according to the colour of their skin, but apparently cats are fair game. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. When I was growing up, we lived in a world of superstitions. We were told not to step on the cracks in the pavement, to avoid the number 13, and to never open an umbrella when indoors. Saying something positive about oneself or hopeful about the future was generally frowned upon. But if you insisted – “hopefully I’ll pass my exams”, “no way will I crash my bike” – you had to immediately say “knock on wood” and then find some wood on which to knock. Since most 1970s houses were constructed from a mix of fibro, brown linoleum and orange Laminex, this was often hard to achieve.



Also, every time someone sneezed you had to say “bless you”, which apparently stopped the devil from using that moment of inattention to enter their soul. If you spilt salt, you also had to throw some over your left shoulder (using your right arm) which had the excellent effect of blinding the devil as he hovered at your shoulder. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. Special occasions such as birthdays were marked by a dinner of roast chicken, the climax of which involved two people grasping the “wish bone” and tearing it in two, good fortune going to the person who ended up with the larger bit of bone. The chicken, already having been throttled, plucked and baked, might have wondered about the purpose of this final indignity, yet it was not possible to eat a chicken while leaving its furcula alone. At Christmas, meanwhile, a silver sixpence would be baked into the Christmas pudding, ready to bring good luck to whoever found it. Or bad luck if you were a seven-year-old and ended up with it stuck in your windpipe, a leading cause of Christmas hospitalisations. The same coin, should it be located in the pudding or returned later by the surgeon, could then be offered as payment for a kitchen knife should you wish to give a knife as a present. It was bad luck to give knives as gifts – it would “cut” the friendship – so the gift had to be turned into a purchase. We were also told we could get rid of warts by “washing our hands in moonlight”, or rubbing them with a piece of meat which you’d then bury in the backyard. If you’ve ever found an old chop bone in your backyard, it was buried there by some warty kid.



You may think this was a charmingly enchanted world, but it did add a lot of fuss to the simplest of tasks, as we were constantly forced to leap over cracks, throw salt over our shoulders, and search for wood to knock upon. In hay fever season, you’d bless more people than the local priest. Related Article Opinion

Health I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Did any of the superstitions make sense? Perhaps a couple. I still avoid walking beneath a ladder, based on the practical consideration that a bucket of paint might be up there somewhere, ready to fall on my head. I also believe that it’s bad luck to put shoes on a table – the bad luck being the transmission of some nasty bug, picked up off the floor of a Sydney bus. As for those low-flying birds at the Sydney Fish Market, I’m betting they did bring good luck. That young woman’s boyfriend was so solicitous, tenderly dabbing her with napkins. It was probably the confirmation for which she’d been hoping: this one was a keeper. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: An ‘informal’ will and the missing jewellery: What will happen to Virginia Giuffre’s $30 million estate?
World.content:
Virginia Giuffre was trying to reclaim control. In early January 2025, she was allegedly assaulted by her husband, Robbie Giuffre, during a family holiday in Dunsborough, Western Australia. Robbie then secured a family violence restraining order against Virginia, which banned the prominent Epstein accuser from contacting her two youngest children for six months. It also meant she was not allowed to go to the family’s beachfront home in Perth, which is where her belongings – including important documents, her memoir manuscript, jewellery and mementos – were kept. So Virginia decided to take back some control and spoil herself.



Virginia’s carer, Cheryl Myers, estimates the mother of three spent about $100,000 at luxury jeweller Linneys, and a local pearl retailer, on jewellery for her mother, and diamond rings and necklaces for herself. She had the money to splurge. As Good Weekend senior writer and Walkley Award-winner Melissa Fyfe and WAtoday journalist Carla Hildebrandt reveal in The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s four-part investigative podcast, Virginia, the payments Virginia received from various confidential settlements with prominent people – such as the man formerly known as Prince Andrew – came to the equivalent of $US25 million ($35.6 million).



What’s remarkable about this shopping spree is not the amount of money Virginia spent. Rather, as Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal in episode four of Virginia – out today – it’s that, more than a year on from Virginia’s death, no one seems to know where the jewellery is. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre “Everybody wants to know about the jewellery,” says Myers. “A couple of days after Virginia had passed, one of Virginia’s friends called me, and asked me, ‘Where was the jewellery?’ And I was like, ‘I’ve got no idea’. “She said, ‘Well, we’ve been to the house, me and Rob, and we’ve looked everywhere for the jewellery, and we can’t find any’. And I said, ‘Well, I don’t know’.” But the jewellery is only one part of the puzzle. Virginia also had a chunk of money in cryptocurrency, and now no one knows what happened to that investment.



Virginia Giuffre is pictured here outside a Manhattan court after Jeffrey Epstein’s death in 2019. She received the equivalent of $US25 million in confidential payments after multiple legal battles over the years. AP Following Virginia’s suicide in April 2025, the rift between her family in the United States, including her two brothers, and Robbie worsened. They are now embroiled in a legal battle over Virginia’s estate, which is estimated to be worth up to $30 million, including the compensation payments, assets, investment properties and book royalties. Virginia, whose divorce from Robbie had not been finalised before her death, died without a valid will. She was supposed to sign it on April 26, 2025 – the day after she died – and had marked this date on the magnetic whiteboard on her fridge. Myers and Virginia’s Perth lawyer, Karrie Louden, say Virginia had an “informal will” expressed to Louden and also emailed to her accountant in February 2025.



“I don’t want Robbie blowing my children’s money on himself.” Virginia Giuffre’s diary notes, written before her death This is backed by Virginia’s brothers and their wives. The “informal will” stipulates a small amount of money going to Virginia’s family and friends, including Myers and her brothers, but the bulk to her children and a small amount to Robbie. They say she wanted the money held in trust until the kids turned 25. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life According to court filings, Virginia’s sons Christian and Noah – backed by their father – are arguing their mother lacked “testamentary capacity” when the informal will was created. If Christian and Noah win, Robbie stands to inherit just over a third of what’s left after the divorce settlement, with the remainder divided between the three children: Christian, Noah, and their daughter.



That would make Robbie the main beneficiary, and most likely the administrator of Virginia’s worldwide estate. “What a terrible, tragic story that everything that she fought for against monsters of sexual assault on the most powerful level, every single dollar is going to go back into the hands of her final abuser, and that’s the last chapter,” says Sky Roberts. “Can we imagine that that’s the way the story ends? Because I can’t, and I can’t live with that.” Listen to the fourth episode of Virginia – where hosts Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal Virginia’s arrest weeks before her death, the real story behind the bus crash that prompted Virginia to tell the world she had days to live, the complicated truth behind her posthumous memoir, and how Virginia’s suicide is part of a wider, systemic problem that is impacting other Australian women – in the player above, wherever you get your podcasts, or click here.



A statement from Robbie Giuffre’s lawyers says the following: “What appears to be an orchestrated attempt by persons to gain financially from Virginia’s death by making unsubstantiated allegations, when they should have been aware of Virginia’s medical conditions, is simply disgraceful. “In the late Virginia Giuffre’s book published and titled Nobody’s Girl, Virginia praised and thanked Robert for his support of her throughout their marriage and in particular, her struggle to be heard.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636.
